2.1 LEFT-WING EXTREMISM
Recommendation
2.1.1 The Committee also notes the death of several security forces personnel in LWE incidents
in 2012. In some cases, it was alleged that the personnel were posted in those areas without
adequate training and the casualties occurred due to non-observance of Standard Operating
Procedures (SOP). The committee feels that these issues need serious consideration and recommends
that the Government should provide adequate training to the personnel of Central Police Forces
as well as State police forces before sending them to LWE affected areas. The Committee also
recommends that these personnel should be equipped with all necessary modern weapons and
security gadgets and the required SOPs should be scrupulously followed by the forces.
(Para 3.6.17 of 169th Report)
Action Taken
2.1.1 ‘Police’ and ‘Public Order’ being State subjects, action with respect to maintenance of law
and order lies primarily in the domain of the State Governments concerned, who deal with the
various issues related to Left Wing Extremist (LWE) activities in the States. The Central
Government monitors the situation closely and supplements and coordinates their efforts in several
ways, inter-alia, including providing Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) to assist the State
Police Forces to deal with the LWE problem.
2.1.2 The CAPF battalions, prior to their induction in the LWE affected States, undergo Counter
Insurgency/pre-induction training at two stages. At the first stage, they undergo pre-induction
training of four weeks with the Army Infantry units and thereafter familiarization/orientation training
of 15 days under the respective State Police.
2.1.3 Besides, in order to strengthen the training inputs of the State Police Forces, the Central
Government has approved establishment of 21 Counter Insurgency and Anti-Terrorist (CIAT)
Schools in the States affected by insurgency and terrorism including Left Wing Extremism. Fifteen
such CIAT Schools have been established/are being established in the LWE affected States of
Bihar (3), Chhattisgarh (4), Jharkhand (4), Odisha (3) and West Bengal (1). The Central
Government also provides assistance to the State Governments in training of State Police Forces
through the Ministry of Defence, Central Police Organisations and Bureau of Police Research and
Development.
2.1.4 W ith regard to provision of modern weapons and gadgets, the Central Government is
providing financial assistance to the State Governments for modernization and upgradation of the
State Police Forces and their intelligence apparatus under the Scheme for Modernization of State
Police Forces (MPF Scheme).
41

42
2.1.5 The State Governments are advised from time-to-time to ensure observance of SOPs by the
security forces deployed in the LWE affected areas.
2.2 NORTH EAST
Recommendation
2.2.1 The Committee is concerned over the prevalence of insurgency in north-east with the
neighbouring countries of the region aiding and abetting ultra-groups in the region. The Committee
notes the large number of surrenders by the underground militants in recent period and is also
aware of the fact that the Government of India has initiated talks with NSC-IM and other militant
groups of the region and hopeful that it will yield desired results soon. The Committee feels that
neighbouring countries of the region should be diplomatically approached and negotiated at highest
level for not allowing their territories for carrying out anti-India activities by insurgent groups of
the region. The Committee understands that several schemes for infrastructural development scheme
are under implementation in the North-East. But the pace of the work is so less that its impact
is not much visible. This needs to change. The Committee is of the firm view that socio-economic
development and expansion of connectivity infrastructure in the North-eastern region only can
counter the ideological influence of the insurgent groups.
(Para 3.7.9 ibid)
Action Taken
2.2.2 The internal security and law and order situation in the North Eastern States, including
insurgencies and talks with various extremist outfits operating in the region as well as security
issues between Indo-Bangladesh and Indo-Myanmar are discussed at the highest level and these
issues are reviewed periodically.
2.3 TERRORISM IN J&K
Recommendation
2.3.1 The Committee notes the claim of the Ministry of Home Affairs that there has been decline
in terrorist violence and infiltration attempts by Pakistan based and aided militants in J&K and
quantum increase in flow of tourists visiting the Kashmir Valley. However, the Committee cautions
the Government from being complacent and to be vigilant constantly as the terrorist infrastructure
in Pakistan/PoK remains intact and infiltration attempts are still being made from across the
border.
(Para 3.8.7 ibid)
Action Taken
2.3.2 The Government has adopted various counter terrorist methods to neutralize the efforts and
capabilities of militants to disturb peace in the State. The Government has also encouraged policies
to mainstream the youth and discourage the local youth from joining militancy.

Recommendation

discriminatory and reminiscent of British colonial era which affects the morale of the forces

(Para 4.1.9 ibid)

Recommendation

3.1 OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF DEMANDS FOR GRANTS
Recommendation
3.1.1 The Committee takes a serious view of the fact that a large quantum of unspent balances
are lying with State Governments under major schemes such as Modernization of State Police
Forces, Special Infrastructure Scheme in LWE affected States etc.. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry should persuade lagging States/UTs to implement the Schemes/
Projects of the Ministry at a fast pace and if the attempts are still not yielding the desired results,
the State Governments may be asked to furnish the Utilization Certificates (UCs) at the earliest.
In case, UCs have become overdue, the amount may be asked to be surrendered or the same may
be adjusted while granting further allocation.
(Para 2.11 of 169
th Report)
Action Taken
3.1.2 The Scheme for Special Infrastructure (SIS) in Left Wing Extremism (LWE) affected
States was approved for implementation during the Eleventh Plan period. The implementation
of the Scheme commenced in the year 2008-09. The works under SIS were sanctioned for
creating necessary infrastructure with a view to enable the security forces to effectively deal
with Left Wing Extremism. During the Eleventh Plan period from 2008-09 to 2011-12, a total
amount of 
R 445.82 crore was released under SIS to the 9 LWE affected States, against
which, Utilization Certificates for R 258.26 crore have been submitted by the 9 LWE affected
States so far.
3.1.3 The works were to be undertaken in remote and severely LWE affected areas. The Progress
of works under the Scheme has been slow due to serious security problems created by the
Maoists, reluctance of contractors to operate in these areas, difficulty in mobilization of material
and machinery resulting in slower utilization of funds. Further owing to changing situations in the
LWE theatre, the CAPFs are required to shift their bases often, which necessitate change of works
approved under SIS leading to delays.
3.1.4 The MHA has been pursuing at all levels for Utilization Certificates and physical and
financial progress report by sending letters/reminders regularly to the State Governments
concerned.
3.1.5 The Ministry of Home Affairs has been taking up the issue of unspent balances lying with
States under the Scheme for Modernization of State Police Forces with the concerned State
Governments from time to time. In various meetings held in MHA, the Ministry has impressed upon
the State Governments to speed up the pace of implementation of the Action Plan approved under
the Scheme and utilize the funds released by the Ministry of Home Affairs for the purpose,
expeditiously.
51

52
3.1.6 The State Governments are requested to furnish Utilization Certificates (UCs) which are due
for rendition to Ministry of Home Affairs timely. The UCs furnished by the State Governments
form the basis for release of grants-in-aid to States under the Scheme in subsequent years. While
processing release of funds to States under the Scheme, the amount of unspent balances lying with
the States for which the UCs have become overdue, is deducted/adjusted by the Ministry of Home
Affairs from the allocations made to the concerned State and the remaining amount is released to
the State.
3.1.7 There is a provision in the Scheme which allows that funds which could not be released
to States due to unspent balances of previous financial years, as on 31
st December of the Financial
Year, may be pooled up and released to better performing States which have a faster pace of
expenditure.
FURTHER OBSERV ATION
3.1.8 The Committee is constrained to express its displeasure that almost half of the
amount allocated during Eleventh Five Year Plan under the Special Infrastructure Scheme
to the State Governments is lying unspent. The Committee understands that
implementation of development projects/schemes in LWE areas is a challenge for the
Government but partial completion of projects would frustrate the very purpose of the
allocations. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry of Home
Affairs should impress upon the State Governments to put all out efforts for optimal
utilization of earmarked allocations in furtherance of execution of developmental projects/
schemes and submit the utilization certificate in time.

Recommendation

the Government in regard to creation of infrastructure of NATGRID. The very proposal of setting
up of NATGRID is still at nascent stage even after a lapse of two years. The Committee
understands that delay in construction of Data centre building of NATGRID would create hurdles
in accomplishing the set objective of the organization. The delay is unacceptable and the project
should pick up pace. The Committee observes that there is no seriousness on the part of Central
Government and, therefore, recommends that the Home Minister or the Cabinet Secretary should
have a meeting with all the concerned Ministries to clear procedural bottlenecks and this project
should take off on immediate basis without any further time and cost overruns.

Action Taken

picture and of events beyond the horizon by collating disjoined pieces of information that exist in
different parts of the environment and stitching them into one view. It will leverage information
technology to access, collate, analyse, correlate, predict and provide speedy dissemination.
3.3.3 Planning Commission has accorded its “in Principle” approval to the project on 08.07.2012,
as a ‘Central Plan Scheme’ under Ministry of Home Affairs from 2011-12. Cabinet Committee on
Security has approved the ‘Detailed Project Report’ (DPR) for an amount of 
R1002.97 crores on
14.06.2012 for Implementation of Foundation, Horizon-I and some elements of Horizon II of the

elements of the NATGRID personnel have been prepared and sent to the Department

of Personnel and Training (DoP&T). Comments of the DoP&T have been received and

(iii) Land has been allotted to NATGRID for Construction of Data Centre (DC & BCP) at

Recommendation
3.4.1 The Committee understands that Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and System

besides strengthening citizen based service delivery system. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Government should complete this project within stipulated time frame for its actual
operationalisation. The Committee is of the strong opinion that the project should not suffer for
want of funds, and therefore, further recommends that enhanced allocation may be made for

55
Action Taken
3.4.2 The prime reason attributed to downsizing is less releases to States/UTs under Grants-in-
Aid. States/UTs have not been released funds because of low utilization of funds already allocated
to them. The Budget had been downsized from the initial Budget Estimates of v 400 crores in year
2012-13 to the Revised Estimates of 
R 85 crores.
3.4.3 The project implementation schedule of Crime and Criminal Tracking Network Systems
(CCTNS) project to be implemented in the Eleventh plan (2007-12) was proposed for four years
(2008-12). The schedule for four years was primarily based on a rationale that project activities
shall be undertaken by diverse stakeholders and would be successfully completed within the
proposed time. The various reasons for the delay are as follows:
● The CCTNS project is based on the principle of “Bundle of Services” wherein a
“System Integrator”(SI) would provide turnkey implementation of all the services
which will constitute implementation of a project in a State/UT. There has been
considerable delay in signing of the SI contract at State/UT level.
● The CCTNS project was conceptualized with a view to leverage the existing IT
infrastructure and network being developed under the other schemes of Department of
Electronics and Information Technology (DeitY) such as SWAN (State Wide Area
Network), SDC (State Data Centre), NSDG (National Service Delivery Gateway) etc.
However, there is a considerable delay in the completion of the above mentioned
schemes when aligned with the proposed implementation schedule of CCTNS project
from the year 2008-12.
● The project initiation activities of CCTNS project in terms of project conceptualization,
preparation of State Plans, preparation of project guidelines, templates, RFPs and other
key project guidance documents which should have been ready in the year 2008-09 for
timely initiation of the project before the approval of CCEA note, were mostly complete
only by the end of the financial year of 2009-10.
● The Core Application Software (CAS) of CCTNS project should have been completed
for initiation of rollout in the year 2009-10 as envisaged in the CCEA note. However
the Software Development Agency (SDA) at the Central level was selected only by
June, 2010 after a bid process which started in August, 2009. The latest build of CAS
has been released to States/UTs only in Dec, 2012.
3.4.4 The work of Project implementation is in full swing across the country. Also, provided that
the Project Implementation deadline is 30th June/31st August, 2013, all States/UTs shall need to
make pending payments to System Integrator, State Project Management Unit (SPMU) and BSNL
in the next few months itself, hence the Ministry shall require more funds to be sanctioned/released
to States/UTs who inturn shall make the respective payments.
Current Status of the Project implementation and action taken to ensure progress as per timelines:
3.4.5 All States/UTs have been given a mandate to finish the CCTNS Project Implementation by

achieve the timelines and also to help them utilize the funds released to them. Some such steps
are:–
● Regular meetings at Home Secretary /AS/JS levels are being held with State Nodal
officers/System Integrators(SIs) /SPMUs and BSNL to monitor and push the progress
in each respect.

56
● Regular visits are being made by National Crime Research Bureau (NCRB) and CPMU
to review the progress in various States/UTs. NCRB and MHA has been intervening in
any matter that States/SIs or SPMUs need help with.
● In order to facilitate faster implementation by the SIs, payment terms are being revised
for SIs, which shall ensure that SIs have the needed cash flow and hence can
continue to work to meet the prescribed timelines.
3.4.6 Below paragraphs detail the Status of implementation of the project:
(a) Selection of System Integrator (SI) by all the States/UTs: 31 State/UTs have till date
signed their respective System Integrator (SI) contracts and 1 State has issued Letters
of Intent to the respective SI. The resources have been deployed by the SIs at the

May 2013 and BSNL is currently working on providing network connectivity at the

(d) Capacity Building: District Training Centre (DTC), Regional training Centre (RTC),

(e) Financial Aspects: Total funds of 
R 446.54 crores have been released to States/UTs as
Grants-in-Aid under the CCTNS project till date, out of which Rs 202.25 crores have

3.5 BORDER MANAGEMENT
Recommendation
3.5.1 The Committee understands the hurdles coming in the way of fencing, construction of roads
etc. due to difficulties in terms of acquisition of land, difficult terrain, non-cooperation from
bordering countries etc. The Committee is of the view that the Government should sort out all these
bottlenecks at the earliest and complete remaining works of fencing and flood lighting as targeted
in a given timeframe. The Committee recommends that the Government should diplomatically
approach and negotiate with the Bangladesh Government for border fencing within 150 yards along
Indo-Bangla Border. An early decision may be taken in the matter.
(Para 3.14.22 ibid)

57
Action Taken
3.5.2 Indo-Bangladesh Border Road passing through Dampa Tiger Reserve (DTR), Mizoram: A
stretch of about 59 km. (BP-2305 to 2313) for construction of border roads along Indo-Bangladesh
Border, falls within the territory of DTR, Mamit district in Mizoram is pending for Forest/
Environment clearance. MoEF clearance is being expedited by the State Government with the
concerned State Wild Life Board (SWLB) and National Board for Wild Life (NBWL) keeping in
view the importance of national security. Their response is awaited in the matter.
3.5.3 Land acquisition:- Execution of works covering about 95 km of border length under
Phase-II project has been adversely affected due to pending land acquisition (LA). This includes
79.58 km. in West Bengal, 11.31 km. in Tripura and 4.11 km. in Mizoram. Although, land
acquisition issues are being regularly monitored/reviewed by the MHA, the problem has persisted
over the years and, given heightened public sensitivities, States have been making slow progress.
The executing agencies viz. CPWD, EPIL and NBCC have been advised to expedite the same in
coordination with the concerned State Governments and BSF.
3.5.4 Delay on account of public protests:- In Meghalaya, construction works under Phase-II
project, in a stretch of about 133 km., has remained suspended for long due to protest by the
Coordination Committee on International Border (CCIB) of Meghalaya. Following continuous
persuasion by MHA, matter in respect of 62.55 km has been sorted out in November, 2011 and
work resumed. With further persuasion with the State Government, stretches of 7 km more have
been sorted out subsequently. Issues including land acquisition for the balance stretches of
63.45 km. are still to be resolved before work commences. A.D.O. letter from JS(BM) has been
addressed to the Chief Secretary, Meghalaya, with the request to convene a meeting to sort out
the above-mentioned issues.
3.5.5 Issues of Fencing within 150 yards of the international borders:- Fencing is generally
constructed beyond 150 yards of the IBB. However, due to existence of population within 150
yards of the IBB and also topographical constraints, it has sometimes been necessary to undertake
fencing within 150 yards of the IBB. This activity has been objected to by Bangladesh. India has
been trying to persuade Bangladesh Government through meetings at different levels  viz.  Home
Secretary, Foreign Secretary, DG/ BSF that the proposed fencing is for the mutual benefit of both
the countries and will help in curbing illegal cross-border activities.
3.5.6 Earlier there were 46 such identified priority patches, and subsequently 185 priority patches
were identified by BSF. It is also stated that both the Border Guarding Forces of the countries
undertake joint survey of these patches. Accordingly, the total priority patches comes to 231. Till
now 129 have been jointly been surveyed by BSF and BGB for fencing within 150 yards from IB.
Patches which need not to be covered are 92 and 10 patches are still required to be jointly
surveyed by BSF and BGB.
Measures adopted by the Government to sort out the problems related to land acquisition, public
protest and 150 yards
3.5.7 The problems of land acquisition and public protest in Meghalaya and Tripura are being
settled by active participation of Land Revenue department of the concerned State Government,
executing agency and BSF. The role of Coordination Committee on International Border (CCIB) is
also important in this case.
3.5.8 MoEF clearance is being expedited by the State Government with the concerned State Wild
Life Board (SWLB) and National Board for Wild Life (NBWL) keeping in view the importance of
national security.

in the agreement on the issue of repatriation of Sri Lanka Refugees. The Committee understands that
this is very sensitive issue where two countries with ethnic overlapping are involved and the
rehabilitation process would take a long time. The Committee observes that 99,469 refugees have been
repatriated back to Sri Lanka upto March, 1995, and thereafter, there is no organized repatriation.
In view of the large influx of Tamil refugees, the Committee is of the view that the approach of the
Government of India should be to see that the influx of refugees should be discouraged and they
should be rehabilitated in their own homeland of Sri Lanka. The Committee in this regard notes that
as a follow up action decided in the Inter-ministerial meeting, a joint inter-ministerial delegation was
to visit camps in Tamil Nadu in January-February, 2012, but its visit is yet to be materialized. The
Committee understands that other course of actions are to be followed up on the findings of the
delegation. This reflects non-seriousness of the Government in redressing the problem. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the course of action as decided in the inter-ministerial meeting held by
Ministry of External Affairs be pursued in the right earnest. The Government should try to prevail
upon the Sri Lankan Government to create conditions conducive for their return.
(Para 5.8.15 ibid)
Action Taken
3.11.2 The Ministry has already requested the State Government of Tamil Nadu as well as the
Ministry of External Affairs to finalize the programme and date for visit of joint inter-ministerial
delegation to the refugee camps in Tamil Nadu to assess the desire of Sri Lankan refugees in India
to return to Sri Lanka and ascertaining the kind of facilitation they expect for this. The Ministry
of External Affairs has also been requested to follow up the action as decided in the inter-ministerial
meeting.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
3.11.3 The Committee is not at all satisfied with the reply. In spite of its recommendation,
no visit of Joint-inter-Ministerial delegation to the camps, till date, has taken place. The
Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation and strongly desires that all necessary
steps be taken to mitigate the sufferings of Tamil refugees.

3.13 DISASTER MANAGEMENT
Recommendation
3.13.1 The Committee in its 161
st report had observed that a specialized force like National

65
Disaster Response Force (NDRF) having 10 battalions only, for entire country, will not serve the
purpose and recommended for raising more battalions of this force. The Ministry in its Action
Taken Reply had mentioned that a draft Cabinet Note for raising of two Additional NDRF
battalions by conversion of two SSB battalions has been prepared by NDRF and the total battalions
of NDRF will be raised to 12. The Committee in its 165th Report on ATR of the Government then
observed that conversion of two SSB battalions into NDRF will not be right approach as it would
affect working of SSB and recommended to the Government to explore other sources to raise
additional battalions of NDRF . The Ministry in its written reply has mentioned that 10 Battalions
of National Disaster Response Force have been constituted for the purpose of specialist response
to disasters and are located at 10 strategic places across India. The Committee is constrained to
observe that the Government has done very little in compliance with the recommendations of the
Committee. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Government should raise more
Battalions of NDRF for responding to disasters.
(Para 5.12.10 ibid)
Action Taken
3.13.2 The Ministry of Home Affairs has taken the decision of raising two new NDRF battalions
converted from SSB battalions in Sept. 2009. To provide prompt response to the South-Western
area of the country, it was decided by the Ministry to station the new NDRF battalion in Karnataka
to take care of parts of Kerala and Karnataka. For providing response to the North-Eastern part
of the country, one NDRF battalion has already been deployed at Guwahati. On requisition of the
State Government of Assam, NDRF battalion deployed at Guwahati provides response to the Upper
Assam during any disaster situation.
3.13.3 Though NDRF is a specialized and well-equipped Force, it is a fact that it is not meant to
the first responder in a disaster. The task of first response is always discharged by the official
machinery of the concerned State Government/UT administration. It is therefore our endeavour to
encourage State Government to develop their own State Disaster Response Force (SDRF). It is also
necessary for the State Governments to pool in their resources, from Home Guards, Civil Defence,
Fire Services, State Red Cross, Nav Yuvak Kendra, National Cadet Corps and National Social
Service V olunteers so that the Disaster Management apparatus is kept in a constant and high state
of preparedness.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
3.13.4 The Committee is not satisfied with the vague reply submitted by the Government
with regard to raising more battalions of NDRF for responding to disasters. The Committee
reiterates that there should not be conversion of SSB battalions or battalions of other para-
military forces as it would badly affect the working of SSB or other para-military forces.
The Committee is of the considered view that there should be other sources for creating
additional battalions of NDRF.

for fencing, construction of roads along Indo-Bangladesh Borders. The Committee
recommends that MHA must undertake follow-up action with Land Revenue Department of
concerned State. (Para 3.5.10)
INDO-TIBETAN BORDER POLICE
The Committee expresses concern that due to shortfall in allocation against the
projected demand meant for ITBP in BE 2012-13, the works of newly raised formation as
well as day-to-day requirement of augmentation of existing establishment suffered. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission
must keep in mind the actual requirement of forces while deciding demands of Ministry of
Home Affairs. (Para 3.6.4)
CENTRAL INDUSTRIAL SECURITY FORCE
The Committee takes note that the inadequate budgetary allocation in 2013-14 under
Plan Scheme at Office Building and Residential Building is adversely affecting development
work of CISF. Therefore, the Ministry of Home Affairs must take up the matter on priority
basis with the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance for their active
consideration and positive decision. The Committee also recommends that Government must
come forward with Modernisation Plan-II for CAPF as it has been approved by CCS in May,
2013 and operationalise the same without much delay. (Para 3.7.4)
DELHI POLICE
The Committee expresses its displeasure over the fact that out of reduced amount
of 
R 0.22 crores, an amount to the tune of R 0.12 crore was still left unspent by Delhi Police
for induction of latest technology in the year 2012-13. The Committee would like to know
the reasons for this. The Committee, however, recommends that the Government should
ensure that the enhanced allocation for financial year 2013-14 for induction of latest
technology in Delhi Police is spent. A sincere monitoring is required in this regard.
(Para 3.8.3)
The Committee feels that women can participate in all walk of life at par with men
successfully and there are ample articles and studies to suggest this. The Committee is,
therefore, of the view that Government should bring forth necessary amendment in the
Recruitment Rules for paving way for employment of women in CAPFs. (Para 3.8.13)
HOUSING SCHEME
The Committee is constrained to note that the housing satisfaction level in CAPF is
dismally low i.e. 16% against the present norms of 25 per cent which has led to higher level
of stress amongst CAPFs personnel as they are not in a position to keep their families with
them. The Committee feels the nature of stresses under which the para-military personnel
perform in difficult terrains. In view of this, the Committee recommends that the Finance
Ministry/Planning Commission should positively consider the additional requirement for
housing scheme at Supplementary stage/re-appropriation stage and also during mid-term
appraisal of the Plan scheme. (Para 3.9.4)

76
FORENSIC SCIENCES LABORATORIES
The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs must expedite the
processing of the Twelfth Plan Proposal of Directorate of Forensic Science Services (DFSS)
for strengthening and upgrading forensic Science Facility in the States. Keeping in view the
important role being played by Forensic Science Laboratories to investigate the complex
nature of crime the Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that Planning
Commission may consider to allocate requisite funds for opening of 06 RFSLs and
52 DMFUs during Twelfth Plan. (Para 3.10.3)
REHABILITATION OF REPATRIATES FROM SRI LANKA
The Committee is not at all satisfied with the reply. In spite of its recommendation,
no visit of Joint-inter-Ministerial delegation to the camps, till date, has taken place. The
Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation and strongly desires that all necessary
steps be taken to mitigate the sufferings of Tamil refugees. (Para 3.11.3)
JAMMU AND KASHMIR
The Committee reiterates that remaining posts be filled up at the earliest. The State
Government may also be impressed upon the need to fill up 3000 posts on its part.
(Para 3.12.4)
DISASTER MANAGEMENT
The Committee is not satisfied with the vague reply submitted by the Government
with regard to raising more Battalions of NDRF for responding to disasters. The Committee
reiterates that there should not be conversion of SSB battalions or battalions of other para-
military forces as it would badly affect the working of SSB or other para-military forces.
The Committee is of the considered view that there should be other sources for creating
additional battalions of NDRF. (Para 3.13.4)
DAMAN AND DIU
The Committee is constrained to express its displeasure that despite its repeated
recommendations for timely completion of seven bridges across the rivers and one signature
bridge connecting Moti Daman and Nani Daman nothing substantial have been achieved. The
Committee is anguished to find that the construction of bridges at Jampore, Kadaiya,
Bamanpuja are yet to see the light of the day because land for the purpose could not be
acquired. While projects pertaining to construction of bridges at Magarwada and Kachigam
have been submitted to Ministry of Road, Transport and Highways. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs must pursue the matter with the
concerned authority and the earliest so that all the projects are completed without much
procrastination. (Para 3.14.3)
The Committee notes the reply. The Committee recommends that the MORTH should
be persuaded to include the project on National Highway Connectivity in the next year.
(Para 3.14.7)
ANDAMAN & NICOBAR ISLANDS
The Committee takes a very serious exception to the very casual reply of the
Ministry. The Committee had sought outcome of the meeting, but the Ministry, to the

77
reasons best known to it, choose to skirt the main thrust of the Committee’s
recommendation. (Para 3.15.3)
The Committee is not satisfied with the action taken as it seems that only Union
Territory administration of Andaman & Nicobar held review meeting with the concerned
public representative. The Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry of Home
Affairs to suggest to other Union Territory administrations also to hold review meeting with
the concerned Members of Parliament. (Para 3.15.6)

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred Seventy-fifth Report on Action Taken by Government on the
observations/recommendations contained in the One Hundred and Seventieth Report on Demands
for Grants (2013-14) of the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region.
2. The One Hundred and Seventieth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Home Affairs was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 25
th April and laid on the Table
of the Lok Sabha on 26 th April, 2013.
3. The Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region furnished the Action Taken Notes on
the One Hundred Seventieth Report. The Minister of Development of North Eastern Region laid the
statement on the status of implementation of the recommendations contained in the said Report of
the Committee on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 10
th December, 2013, pursuant to the Chairman,
Rajya Sabha’s Direction dated 24 th September, 2004.

Seventieth Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants (2013-14) of the Ministry. The One
Hundred Seventieth Report was presented to Rajya Sabha/laid on the Table of Lok Sabha, on the
25
th/26th April, 2013.
2. Action Taken Notes as received from the Ministry of DoNER in respect of the
recommendations contained in the One Hundred and Seventieth Report have been categorized as
follows:
Chapter–I: The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the
Government: Para Nos. 2.3.4, 2.3.7, 2.4.8, 2.4.9, 2.5.3, 2.6.6, 2.7.15, 2.7.16, 2.8.14,
2.8.15, 2.9.8, 2.9.17, 2.9.18, 2.10.6, 2.10.7, 2.11.6, 2.13.6, 2.13.9, 2.14.5, 3.2.4, 3.3.9,

Hundred and Seventieth Report) Total recommendations – 32
The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has accepted its thirty one
recommendations as mentioned in Chapter-I of the Report.
Chapter–II: The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to
pursue in view of the Government’s replies: Para Nos. 2.3.11, 2.12.5, 2.15.4, 3.1.2, 3.3.11

1.1 PROJECTED DEMAND IN THE BUDGET 2013-14
Recomendation
1.1.1 The Committee notes with concern that against the projected Demand of Ministry of DoNER
for the year 2013-14 of R 3614.91 crore only R 2006.00 crore has been approved. The Committee
wonders as to also how the Ministry will make up for such a huge deficit of
R 1608.91 crore and recommends the Ministry to take up the matter with the Planning Commission
and Ministry of Finance to enhance allocation at the RE Stage so that originally envisaged course
of actions are undertaken with enhanced allocation. This will, however, depend on the expenditure
pattern.
(Para 2.3.4 of 170th Report)
Action Taken
1.1.2 The observations/recommendations of the Committee have been noted. The matter regarding
enhancement of allocation, depending on the expenditure pattern, will be taken up with the Planning
Commission and Ministry of Finance at the RE Stage.
FURTHER OBSERV ATION
1.1.3 The Committee would like to be apprised of the outcome of efforts made by Ministry
of DoNER regarding enhancement of allocation at RE stage of 2013-14.
1.2 NORTH EASTERN CLIMATE CHANGE ADOPTION-PROJECT
Recomendation
1.2.1 The Committee feels that the Ministry should have presented its case before the Planning
Commission more strongly to get its proposed 12th Plan outlays approved. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry should improve its absorption capacities so that it can demand more
funds for various projects. The Committee finds that adverse effects of climate change in NE
Region can be seen from decreasing rain fall in the region and increasing melting of glaciers. In
view of the Committee, the NE Region has become highly vulnerable to the consequences of
climate change and the adaptation as well as mitigation projects are the need of the hour. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that Planning Commission should also consider allocating funds
for North East Climate Change Adaptation Project.
(Para 2.3.7 ibid)
Action Taken
1.2.2 It is submitted that North Eastern Climate Change Adaptation Project (Financial Co-operation)
is being considered by Government of India under Indo-German Co-operation in five North Eastern
2

3
States, namely, Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Mizoram and Sikkim. The overall project cost is
Euro 99.7 million and the project duration is 7 years. The financing mechanism requires
reimbursement method of payment, i.e., the upfront payment for the project activities have to be
made by Government of India through Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region securing
about 6% contribution from the States and 5% contribution from the State communities, both
purely in kinds. At the time of budget estimate proposals, the project was not ready for
implementation. Certain critical issues like creation of Regional Society and its location and funding
mechanisms were not finalised. Therefore, it was decided to present the budget requirement to the
Planning Commission after Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) approves the proposal. It is
noteworthy that ‘No objection’ from all concerned line Ministries has been obtained including from
Planning Commission. At this stage, Planning Commission has been requested for ‘in principle’
approval and budget allocation for the project following which steps shall be taken to obtain final
approval of Government of India.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
1.2.3 The Committee notes the reply and desires that the Planning Commission should
give ‘in principle’ approval at the earliest.
1.3 NORTH-EASTERN COUNCIL
Recomendation
1.3.1 The Committee, while noting that the success of NEC efforts depends heavily on the
cooperation from the State Governments, feels that the Council should evolve an incentive structure
for better performance so that performing States could be motivated to do better and non-
performing States may be made to feel that they may loose on account of non-performance.
(Para 2.4.8 ibid)
Action Taken
1.3.2 The suggestion of the Committee has been noted and steps would be taken to evolve an
incentive structure for better performance of States.

projects on time despite very short working season in the North East Region as one cannot alter
the geographical cycles. The Committee recommends that NEC may conduct a comparative study

similar handicaps. The Committee also notes unavailability of raw material as well as limited
capacity of contractors and executing agencies. The Committee feels that the Government should
come forward to address those deficiencies affecting execution of the projects in NER by
augmenting supply of raw material and assistance to the executing agencies by providing soft loans
to them.
(Para 2.4.9 ibid)
Action Taken

direction of the Committee to address the deficiencies affecting execution of projects in NER.

CORPORATION (NERAMAC)
Recomendation
1.6.1 Given its mandate of encouraging food processing units in NER and providing basic
infrastructure for marketing of agricultural and allied products, the allocation of 
R 2.00 crore for

5
BE 2013-14 to NERAMAC is too low for carrying out its activities. The Committee notes that the

Recomendation
1.8.1 The Committee is highly dismayed and extremely dissatisfied with the abysmal rate of
completion of projects under the scheme. The Committee was given similar excuses for non-
performance during the consideration of Demands for Grants (2012-13) wherein it noted in its
recommendation given in 162nd Report. The same set of excuses are again being given this year
like delay in tendering process, delay in transfer of funds to implementing agencies, delay in
utilization of funds and timely non-submission of correct and proper documents by State
Governments etc. The Committee feels that nothing has changed on ground except for tall promises
to rectify the situation. The Committee strongly recommends that the various steps mooted by the
Ministry should be implemented immediately so that marked improvement gets visible in real terms

of 
R. 514.29 crore.
FURTHER OBSERV ATION
1.8.3 The Committee views that intensive monitoring of progress of implementation of
projects under NLCPR scheme would definitely result in achievement of set targets.

1.14 NORTH EASTERN REGION LIVELIHOOD PROJECT (NERLP)-EAP
Recomendation
1.14.1 The Committee appreciates the role of NERLP in preparing the community institutions for
self governance, bottom up planning, democratic functioning with transparency and accountability.
The Committee desires that community based institutions under the project must be encouraged in
larger numbers for sustainable agricultural and natural resource management. The Committee
believes that participation of Self Help Groups (SHGs) as Community Service Providers (CSPs)
would go a long way in achieving the set objective of the NERLP . The Committee therefore,
recommends that concerted efforts must be made in this direction.
(Para 2.13.9 ibid)

10
Action Taken
1.14.2 The following initiatives are being taken in NERLP:
(a) The Project proposes to create strong community institutions. It will give emphasis on
formation of sustainable and vibrant primary institutions of the poor based on the
principle of thrift and credit as women Self Help Groups (SHGs), Youth Groups and
Producers Groups. The villages will be covered to saturation level.
(b) Several SHGs will form Village Federation to promote self-reliant and financial
independence which will be sustainable. Federations would partner with variety of
organizations for linkages to market institutions and provide delivery mechanisms for
various Government programs.
(c) Youth Groups with primary level educations would be formed and given special sector
skills for employability.
(d) Community Development Groups would try to address livelihood gaps of the poor and
vulnerable section of community. They will aggregate the needs and demands and
provide a platform to effectively engage in decision making process for economic
empowerment for self-reliant, self-managed and sustainable livelihood improvement for
community.
(e) Producer’s Organizations would be formed at village level by drawing members from
SHGs, YGs and SDSs. They would have their own internal working arrangements with
distribution of work tasks, responsibilities for hiring outside professionsl, various
technical and specialist tasks. Capacity building inputs would be provided to Board
members for running commercial organization.
(f) Market linkages would be established so that producer’s organizations and individual
producers are able to get good return for their produce. Project will tie up with ICAR
Research Labs, CSIR research stations to provide technical knowledge and expertise
to organizations. This sector support organization will provide assistance for value
chain which will help producers to aligne their produce to market requirements.
(g) Livelihood activities taken up by NERLP would be complimented by MGREGA which
has much needed support for farmers with upfront capital for management of natural
resources in the form of water conservation and forest protection.
(h) The process of community mobilization has been initiated and concerted efforts are
being taken to bring transformational changes in the project states.

1.16.2 Accelerating pace of completion of infrastructure projects in NER was reviewed by the

implementation of existing projects by strengthening project execution capabilities on
the ground, stationing NHAI staff close to the field and regular review by the Ministry

1.21 INLAND WATER CONNECTIVITY
Recomendation
1.21.1 The Committee understands the importance of Inland Waterways as an alternative to other
modes of transport which are found lacking in many parts of the region. Inland waterways has
huge potential which can also be used to supplement the existing routes on land. Waterways are
the cheapest mode of transport anywhere in the world. In Western European countries, about 40
per cent of the cargo movement is by waterways. The world’ s average is about 8 per cent, whereas
in India it is less than 1 per cent. The Committee is surprised to find that in the National Water
Policy, navigation comes almost towards the end on the list of priority. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that navigation in NER should find priority as it is not only an economical mode of
transport but also eco-friendly and there is immense scope for improvement in the field of Inland
Waterways in NER. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry of Shipping
along with Ministry of Water Resources should pursue all the projects vigorously in close
coordination with the Ministry of DoNER. The Committee also recommends that fund constraints
should not come in the way of the implementation of projects. The Committee also recommends that
Inland Water Transport projects in Tripura, Meghalaya and Mizoram which are at various stages
of planning may be expedited and finalised.
(Para 3.8.3 ibid)

3.3 POTENTIAL OF HYDRO-ELECTRIC (HE) PRODUCTION IN NE REGION
Recomendation
3.3.1 The Committee is at a loss to understand that despite such elaborate planning and huge
administrative mechanism, the realization of the potential remains abysmally low. The Committee
finds that even though Inter-Ministerial Groups (IMG), Task Force, Advisory Groups and Special
Monitoring Groups (SMG) were set up by the Government at one point of time or other to sort
out the problems afflicting the projects, yet perceptible outcome is still a distant dream.
(Para 3.3.7 ibid)
Action Taken
3.3.2 A number of steps and Policy measures have been taken by the Government in order to give
a thrust to the development of hydro electric potential in the country especially in the NE Region.
The basic objective of constitution of various Committees and Groups at different levels is to
formulate policies/guidelines for accelerated development of hydro-power and to examine, discuss
and resolve the issues impeding the development of hydro-power in the country. It may be
appreciated that development of hydro-electric projects is an intricate and long drawn process
spanning over 3-5 years. Long time is required for survey and investigation, preparation of DPR,
obtaining of statutory and non statutory clearances including environment and forest clearances,
concurrence by CEA, investment decision and financial closure. Once the projects achieve financial
closure, implementation takes another 5-8 years. Thus, hydro projects usually have long gestation
period and require larger capital investment. This inherent long gestation period of a hydel project
coupled with unforeseeable reasons such as land acquisition problems, environment and forest
issues, extent of Resettlement and Rehabilitation problems, Law and Order problem and geological
surprises further slows down the development of hydro-power.
3.3.3 It may also be mentioned that hydro projects are site specific and located in difficult/
inaccessible sites. The reasons for slow pace of growth in the region, besides the inapproachability,
is attributed to the fact that as the demand of power in the region is low, the development of hydro
power potential was not taken up on a large scale. Now, with the interconnection of regional grids,
the power from N.E. Region could be transported to other energy deficit regions of the country.
The development of infrastructure like road etc. is also getting priority in N.E. Region which would
help in expeditious harnessing of hydro potential.

31
3.3.4 In the Eleventh plan, 163 MW of generation capacity addition was achieved in the NER and
510 MW in Sikkim as against a target of 663 MW in NER and 699 MW in the state of Sikkim.
3.3.5 In the Twelfth Plan, a capacity addition target of 3530 MW has been planned in the NER
(3348 in the central sector and 182MW in the state sector) and 2066 MW for Sikkim (all in the
private sector). So far, 663 MW capacity addition has been achieved (407 MW in Central, 87 MW
in State and 169 MW in Private Sectors).
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS
3.3.6 The Committee strongly recommends that serious efforts are required for
furtherance of execution of hydro-power projects and achievement of set objectives. The
Committee reiterates its observations that accelerated development of hydro-power projects
in NER would not only ensure balanced regional economic growth but would also facilitate
transmission of power to other energy deficit part of the country. The Committee, in this
regard, recommends that the delay in execution of hydro-power projects is to be tackled
through resilient strategy with strong administrative will.
3.4 POTENTIAL OF HYDRO-ELECTRIC (HE) PRODUCTION IN NE REGION
3.4.1 The Committee finds that while the identified potential in NE Region constitutes about
40.1% of the total identified hydro power potential (145320 MW) in the country, but only 1200
MW has so far been harnessed in NE region which is 2.06% of the identified capacity and only
6 HE projects with aggregate capacity of 2852 MW (4.89%) are under construction in NER. Even
if the under construction projects in the region are completed on time, the potential likely to be
realized will only be close to 7%. This leaves a huge gap between potential capacity and potential
realized. In an energy deficit country like ours, this is totally unacceptable. The Committee feels
that the huge bureaucratic mechanism put in place for the purpose and the policy guidelines
adopted by themselves are not enough and a spirited effort is required to make things happen on
the ground. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a very practical approach with quantifiable
progress indicators should be adopted for progress on ground.
(Para 3.3.8 ibid)
Action Taken
3.4.2 The hydro potential of North Eastern Region, including Sikkim is 62604 MW (above
25 MW). At present, 13 H.E. Projects (above 25 MW Capacity) with an installed capacity of 1911
MW (3.05 %) are in operation and 14 H.E. Projects (above 25 MW Capacity) with an installed
capacity of 5132 MW (8.19%) are under construction in NER, including Sikkim.
3.4.3 In addition, a total of 124 H.E. Schemes (above 25 MW) with an aggregate capacity of
48932 MW including HE Projects Cleared (21 Nos., 18672 MW) and under Examination in CEA
(11 Nos., 4692 MW) have been allotted to Central, State and Private Sector for implementation
during Twelfth Plan and beyond in the NER including Sikkim.
3.4.4 As regard the recommendations of the Committee that a very practical approach with
quantifiable progress indicators should be adopted for progress on ground, it is stated that most
of the yet to be developed hydro power potential sites are situated in remote and inaccessible
locations, having the most inclement weather conditions full of challenges on all fronts – logistics,
climatic, technological leading to long gestation period of 5-10 years and as such are subject to
more or less similar challenges in terms of risk of occurrence of hydrological, geological, socio-
economical uncertainties, R&R issues besides delay in statutory clearances especially MOEF
clearance, law and order problems, etc.

32
3.4.5 However, some of the issues like geological surprises, local agitation and other law and
order related problems can not be foreseen in advance, leading to delay in commissioning of some
of the affected projects. Whenever, such unforeseen problems are reported by the project
authorities in the Central, State or Private Sector, immediate remedial steps are taken as per the
requirement of each project on a case to case basis e.g. for sorting out law and order problem,
the issue is immediately brought to the notice of the State law enforcing agencies.
3.4.6 Government of India has been taking proactive initiatives like the new Hydro policy,
coordination and follow up with the concerned Ministries/departments for expediting clearances,
greater monitoring etc. The projects which are under development are likely to come up during the
Thirteenth Plan and beyond. It is evident that the new Hydro Policy, 2008 has started showing its
impact, however, due to the long gestation period of hydro projects, its full impact would get
reflected on the ground from Thirteenth Plan onwards.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
3.4.7 The Committee understands the geographical and geological constraints. Since energy
is the basic input for economic development projects, concerted and co-ordinated approach
and resilient strategy is required for maximum harnessing of identified hydro power
potential. More pro active efforts are the need of the hour to achieve the targets.

Board is the Member who is incharge of all Railway Projects including projects in the North East.
He is regularly reviewing implementation of all Railway Projects including those in North East on
regular basis by way of scrutiny/monthly progress reports of all projects, holding quarterly
meetings with construction officials of concerned Railway. In addition, review meetings are also
held.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
3.7.3 The Committee would like to highlight that the then Chairman, Railway Board
mentioned about the inadequacy of the funds before the Committee on 10
th June, 2013.
When the matter was taken up with the then Expenditure Secretary who appeared before
the Committee on 4
th July, 2013, he submitted that there was no paucity of funds for
sustainable infrastructural projects provided the line Ministries enhanced capability
absorption for better execution of undertaken projects. Thereon, the Committee had in its
173
rd Report (para 5.22) recommended that a meeting of concerned senior officers of the
Railways Board, Planning Commission, Ministry of Finance may be called to sort out the
issue of constrains of resources to fund National projects. The Committee reiterates that
recommendation. Ministry of Railways may take up the matter with Planning Commission
and Ministry of Finance on the resources and resolve the issue at the earliest.
3.8 INLAND WATER CONNECTIVITY
Recomendation
3.8.1 The Committee notes with disappointment that Inland Waterway Terminal of Pandu which
is being developed as multi modal transit system is still hanging fire for want of handing over of
land. The Committee directs that the matter should be taken up with the NF Railway and resolved
as soon as possible. The Committee further recommends that work on proposed roll-on-roll-off
terminals at Dhubri and Hatsingimari be started immediately without further delay. CPWD may
take up the work on priority.
(Para 3.8.4 ibid)

35
Action Taken
3.8.2
● With regard to the approach road to Pandu terminal through NF railway land (6210 sq.
m.), IWAI has already paid the entire lease amount of R 3.45 crore to NF railway. NF
railway could not hand over the land due to unauthorized encroachment. IWAI and
District Administration had suggested an alternative alignment. However, Railway
Authorities declined the proposal.
● With regard to construction of Roll on Roll off (Ro-Ro) terminal at Dhubri and
Hatsingimari the work has already been awarded to CPWD in January, 2013. The cost
of construction of Dhubri terminal would be 
R 28.98 crore, where as for the
Hatsingimari Terminal it would be R 33.31 core. CPWD has initiated action for
construction of Dhubri terminal. However, due to severe bank erosion in and around
the terminal location at Hatsingimari, Water Resource Department of Assam and
Brahmaputra Board has been requested to consider bank protection work before
commencement of construction at Hatsingimari.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
3.8.3 The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Railway should either accept the
request of IWAI and district administration for alternative alignment to provide the
approach road to Pandu terminal or hand over the land without unauthorized encroachment
to IWAI for development of ‘Inland Waterway Terminal of Pandu’ as ‘multi-modal transit
system’. The Committee further recommends that CPWD must take all steps for early
completion of construction of Roll on Roll off (Ro-Ro) terminal at Dhubri and Hatsingimari.
3.9 TOURISM
Recomendation
3.9.1 The Committee understands that the continuation with special LTC scheme for govt.
employees and creation of necessary human and physical capacities to absorb such demand would
further expand the number of tourists in NER. The Committee would also like to suggest that
government may consider running of tourist trains on viable tourist circuits in the NER, on the
lines of tourist trains already running in other parts of the country.
(Para 3.9.8 ibid)
Action Taken
3.9.2 The matter pertaining to LTC comes under the purview of the Department of Personnel and
Training. In so far as Tourist Trains are concerned, the same comes under the purview of Ministry
of Railways. Both the respective ministries may therefore be addressed in the matter. It may be
noted that under the scheme of Assistance for Large Revenue Generating Projects being
implemented by Ministry of Tourism, tourist trains are eligible for being provided financial
assistance. Central Financial Assistance (CFA) for such projects is considered as and when
proposals are received from State Governments.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
3.9.3 The Committee keeping in view the tourism prospects in NER, recommends that the
Ministry of DoNER should take up the matter of running of tourist trains in NER, with the

36
Ministry of Railway/Ministry of tourism, which in turn may formulate projects and seek
central Financial Assistance for such projects. State Government should also be sensitised
in this regard.
3.10 INDUSTRIAL SECTOR
Recomendation
3.10.1 The Committee believes that the spill-over benefits of industrial development for the region
would be the development of infrastructure such as roads, communications, and electricity supply
to remote hilly areas, resulting in better quality of life. Natural gas based industries are also
feasible. The Committee also believes that NER could be an excellent centre for horticulture,
spices, and hub for educational and IT sector.
(Para 3.10.6 ibid)
Action Taken
3.10.2 To further incentivize the benefits to natural gas based industries, Ministry of Petroleum
and Natural Gas may formulate its schemes to cover such units. Similar schemes can also be
formulated by Ministry of Agriculture, Ministry of Food Processing Industries and Ministry of
Communication and Information Technology for incentivizing units in the field of horticulture,
spices and IT sector.
FURTHER OBSERV ATION
3.10.3 The Committee gets an impression that the ‘Action Taken’ does not give any action
taken by the Government in response to the Committee’s recommendations. The
Committee is not aware whether its recommendation was communicated to the concerned
Ministries or not. The Committee would like to be apprised of the action taken by the
Ministry of DoNER in this regard.

turn would not only lengthen the period of economic growth of NER, but also the very

REPORT
CHAPTER-I
 INTRODUCTION
1.1 Section 3 of the Delhi Police Act, 1978 stipulates that there shall be one police force for
the whole of Delhi and all officers and subordinate ranks of the police force shall be liable for
posting to any branch of the force including the Delhi Armed Police. According to Annual
Report 2012-13 of Ministry of Home Affairs, the priorities of Delhi Police are maintenance of law
and order, prevention of crimes, instilling a sense of security amongst common people including
women, children and senior citizens, improving traffic management and controlling corruption. Top
most priority is given to maintenance of law and order and crime control and emphasis is given
on control of crime through proactive policing with people’s participation.
1.2 Mission Of Delhi Police
1.2.1 According to Citizen’s Charter, the objectives of Delhi Police are as under:–
(i) To uphold the law, fairly and firmly;
(ii) To prevent crime and to pursue and bring to justice those who break the law;
(iii) To keep the peace in partnership with the community;
(iv) To protect, help and reassure the people;
(v) To be seen discharging duty with integrity, common sense and sound judgment;
(vi) To be Compassionate, courteous and patient, acting without fear or favour or
prejudice to the rights of others;
(vii) To be professional, calm and restrained and in the event of mob control, apply
minimum force necessary to accomplish lawful duty;
(viii) To strive to reduce the fears of the public; and
(ix) To respond to well-founded criticism with a willingness to change.
1.2.2 According to the Commissioner of Police, priorities and the main functions of Delhi Police
are as under:–
(i) Keep the capital secure from terror;
(ii) Detect and prevent crime and improve quality of investigation;
(iii) Maintain law and order and protect people under threat;
(iv) Curb street crime;
(v) Build sound police-public relations;
(vi) Initiate measures in collaboration with the community to wean away street-children
and juveniles from committing crime;

2
(vii) Provide a safe environment to working women who work and return during night;
(viii) Looking after the welfare of officers and men;
(ix) Upgrade the capability of the force with high quality training; and
(x) Synergies with traffic engineers, civic agencies and other stakeholders for good traffic
management.
1.3 Brife History of Organisational Structure
1.3.1 As per the information available on Delhi Police website, organized form of policing was
established by the British after the First War of Freedom of 1857, with the adoption of the Indian
Police Act of 1861. Delhi, being a part of the Punjab, remained a unit of the Punjab Police even after
becoming the Capital of India in 1912. In the same year, the first Chief Commissioner of Delhi was
appointed and was vested with the powers and functions of the Inspector General of Police.
1.3.2 Delhi Police was re-organised in 1946 when its strength was almost doubled. In the
year 1966, the Government of India constituted the Delhi Police Commission headed by Justice G.D.
Khosla to go into the problems faced by Delhi Police and it was on the basis of the Khosla Commission
Report that the Delhi Police was once again re-organised. Four police districts, namely, North, Central,
South and New Delhi were constituted. The Khosla Commission also recommended for introduction of
Police Commissioner System which was eventually adopted from 1
st July, 1978. With the passage of
time the population of Delhi and problems of policing kept on multiplying. Accordingly, the strength of
Delhi Police was increased upto about 76,000 as per recommendations of the Srivastava Committee.
At present, there are six ranges, 11 districts, 54 divisions and 184 Police Stations with a total strength
of 83,762 Delhi Police personnel. The Committee is given to understand that Delhi Police is the largest
metropolitan police in the world, larger than London, Paris, New York and Tokyo.
1.3.3 Replying to a query regarding the ratio of Constables, Inspectors and Higher Officers
viz-a-viz. ACP, DCP, etc., the Delhi Police informed the Committee that the ratio between constable
Inspectors, ACP and DCP is as under:
Constable and Inspector = 34 : 01
Constable and ACP = 131 : 01
Constable and DCP = 429 : 01
1.3.4 Replying to the Committee’s query in regard to the ideal ratio of policemen per lakh
populations, Delhi Police stated that no information as to the police and population ratio of other
countries is being compiled by BPR&D. However, as per the report prepared by UN Division for
Policy Analysis and Public Affairs, available on the web site of United Nations, Police-Population
ratio in some of the countries is as follows:– Italy (559.0), Mexico (491.8), Saudi Arabia (386.5)
and Belgium (357.5) which is much higher than in India (143) during the year 2006.
1.3.5 The Committee also sought to know whether any study was conducted /adopted by Delhi Police
on ‘Police Reform’s. The representatives of Delhi Police stated that no such study on Police Reforms
has been conducted. However, reforms are continuous process and necessary measures are taken from
time to time and directions are issued in the form of Circulars/Standing Orders. The Committee was
further apprised that the MHA, Gov ernment of India has set up various Commissions/Committees on
the Police Reforms for all States and Union Territories of India from time to time. The Ministry had
set up a Review Commission to scrutinize the recommendations made by these Commissions/
Committees. On the basis of the recommendations made by the Review Commissions, Ministry of
Home Affairs shortlisted 49 Recommendations and directed all States and Union Territories to implement
the same and Delhi Police has implemented most of these with the approval of MHA.

3
CHAPTER-II
CRIME SITUATION
2.1 According to the background note as furnished by Delhi Police, the law and order situation
in Delhi –2012 is the combined effect of several aspects of police work which inter-alia include
prevention and detection of crime, traffic management, VVIP/VIP security, counter terrorism
measures, handling of protest/agitation/rallies, managing festivals, maintaining police community
relations, surveillance on criminals, public awareness programmes, police response mechanism, etc.
which give the citizens an overall sense of security to carry on with their daily lives.
2.2 Crime Situation
2.2.1 The Committee has noted that Delhi Police is entrusted with the responsibility to ensure a
safe environment to the people living in Delhi especially for working women, senior citizens and
children. According to Delhi Police, during the last 15 years crime has remained under control
despite manifold growth of population in Delhi. It was stated that Delhi Police strives to keep the
Capital secure from terror and detect and prevent crime and improve quality of investigation, curb
street crime, build sound police-public relations and maintain law and order and protect people
under threat.
2.2.2 According to the background note, Delhi Police has undertaken the following new initiatives
to achieve its set objectives:–
(i) High visibility of police by revamping beat police system;
(ii) Integrated police patrolling through PCR, Traffic and local police;
(iii) Deployment of Traffic and local Police Staff at selected Bus Stops for covering 300
Bus Stops for anti-sabotage; checking of Bus Stop; checking of the buses for looking
for unclaimed objects, search of suspicious persons, anti-eve-teasing drive, anti-pick-
pocketing drive etc.;
(iv) Prompt investigation of cases and performance appraisal for all ranks;
(v) ACPs/SDPOs to remain in one police station of their sub division daily between 3.30
PM-5.30 PM; and
(vi) 155 Emergency Response Vehicles in Police Stations make arrangements one in each
PS. These vehicles are first Responder to distress calls, preserve scene of crime using
caution tape, perform Anti-terrorist tasks and ensure higher visibility in PS area.
2.2.3 The Delhi Police claimed that the total IPC Crime per lakh of population has seen a steady
decline during the last 14 years, being 505.71 in 1998 and coming down to 293.13 in 2012. The
number of total heinous offences registered in Delhi in 1998 was 2807, and it came down to 2171
in 2011. Heinous offences per lakh of population declined from 21.88 in 1998 to 14.01 as on
31st October, 2012 which, however, showed increasing trend to 21.79 on 30 th September, 2013.
2.2.4 The Committee was given to understand that in 1998, population of Delhi was 128.3 lakhs
and total IPC crimes were 64882 whereas, while the population rapidly rose to 167.53 lakhs in the
3

4
year 2011, the total IPC crime remained only 53353, thus clearly indicating it was better in 2011
than 14 years back. In geographical terms also, Delhi has grown exponentially and many new
colonies such as Rohini, Dwarka and industrial areas like Narela have come up.
2.3 Causative Factors
2.3.1 Delhi Police apprised the Committee that Delhi, being the capital of the country, has been
developing all around at a rapid pace. This rapid urbanization has also led to certain factors which
have a bearing on the crime rate in the city. The large expansion of new colonies and thousands
of unplanned colonies is also an important crimogenic factor particularly in respect of street crimes
like robberies and snatching. Despite this, the incidents of street crime have come down in the city.
In Delhi, almost 65% of the total population lives in unplanned colonies. 11.7% live in rural/urban
villages, thus leaving only 23.7% people living in planned colonies. This is an important causative
factor for crime in Delhi. Other factors responsible for crime are as follows:–
(i) Socio-economic imbalances;
(ii) Proximity in location of colonies of the affluent and the under-privileged;
(iii) Urban anonymity encouraging deviant behaviour;
(iv) Loosening of social structures and family control;
(v) Adverse sex ratio (866 females/1000 males);
(vi) Easy accessibility/means of escape to criminal elements from across the borders; and
(vii) Extended hinterland in the NCR region.
2.4 Trends of Crimes in Delhi
2.4.1 According to Delhi Police there has been a decline in street crimes in the city in the year
2012 which is a result of enhanced police presence and continuous monitoring of activities of
known criminals. Citing high detection rate achieved in heinous cases, Delhi Police informed the
Committee that a success rate of 85.96% in 2012 and 85.04% in 2013 (upto 30
th September, 2013)
has been achieved as against 91.99 % in year 2011 in heinous offences. This has been achieved
as a result of sustained efforts and police professionalism at the District level and the specialized
units like the Crime Branch and the Special Cell, which whole-heartedly focussed on achieving
breakthroughs, in all important and sensational cases.

th September, 2013)

5
2.4.2 The Committee was further informed that in the year 2012, 521 murder cases had been
registered as against 543 cases in the corresponding period of year 2011. Incidents of murders, per
lakh of population, have also shown a significant decline during the last ten years. While this figure
was 3.95 in the year 2011, it came down to 3.05 in 2012. Explaining about the motives behind
murders, the Committee was informed that an analysis of motives in murder cases of year 2012
reveals that 20.54 % of the cases were due to sudden provocation on trivial issues followed by
12.86% due to old enmity, 14.59% sex related, 10.94% differences amongst family members and
8.83% disputes over property/money matters. About 13.82% of the murder cases were crime related.
2.4.3 Regarding robbery/dacoity, the Committee was informed that in the year 2012 a total of 608
cases of robbery were reported as against 562 cases in the corresponding period of year 2011. The
detection rate in cases of robbery has been high at 88.32%. During the year 2012, a total of 28
cases of dacoity were reported as against 33 cases in the corresponding period of the year 2011,
showing a significant decline of 15.15%. All the cases (except one case) of dacoity reported during
the year 2012 have been solved.
2.4.4 The Committee was also informed that the broad day light sensational dacoity-cum-murder
case in Defence Colony of more than rupees 5 crores cash was solved in a record time with
arrests of 14 persons and recovery of cash of more than 4 crores and other items purchased from
the looted money.
2.4.5 As regards snatching, the Committee was informed that in the year 2012, a total of 1440
cases of snatching were reported as against 1476 cases reported in the year 2011, a decline of
2.44%. As many as 70.97% cases were solved.
2.4.6 App rising about Motor Vehicle Theft, the representative of Delhi Police stated that in the
year 2012, a total of 14391 Motor Vehicle Theft cases have been reported as against 14668 cases
in the year 2011, registering a decline of 1.89 %. 19.78 % cases of stolen vehicles were solved
in the year 2012. The M.V Thefts per lakh of vehicle population has also come down from 228.35
in the year 2001 to 186.97 in 2012. Motor Vehicle Thefts accounted for 28% of total IPC cases
registered in Delhi. The acute shortage of parking space and the general practice of parking
vehicles on roadsides coupled with the indifference of a majority of motor vehicle owners towards
installing anti-auto theft equipment is a major contributory factor.
2.4.7 The Committee observes that the number of rape case reported in Delhi were higher than

2.5.3 The Committee is anguished to find that the conviction rate in criminal cases is
dipping year after year i.e. 69.12% in 2008, 66.46% in 2009, 56.60% in 2010 and 53.19%
in 2011. The Committee observes that the conviction rate of crimes committed and detected
in Delhi is abysmally low and one possible reason could be excessive work load with the
courts, but equally important is the undue extraneous pressure being put on the
investigating agencies thus causing delay in the process of investigation. The Committee is
of the view that as investigating agency, the police force has to shoulder an onerous
responsibility. The fate of any case depends upon the outcome of investigation. The
Committee understands that investigation requires a lot of skills, expertise and in-depth
understanding of jurisprudential principles and legal insight. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the training module of Delhi Police must incorporate advance courses on
law and jurisprudence. The training module of Delhi Police on law and jurisprudence may
be revisited involving some legal experts. Besides, the Committee also recommends that
there is a need to have brain storming session to find out reasons for low conviction rate
and take the remedial measures before the situation further deteriorates.

2.6.1 According to the background note, in regard to tackling the crimes, it was stated that due
attention was given to detective and preventive aspects i.e. integrated patrolling systems with active
participation of PCR vans and special drives launched against eve teasers. Modern scientific and
other techniques were adopted to improve the quality of investigation, quick redressal of public
grievances, active participation of NGOs, follow-up of “Eyes and Ears Scheme”. Roads and lanes/
streets prone to criminal activities, were identified and barricaded besides police personnel patrolling

stated to be as under:

criminals of every Police Station, monitoring and surveillance of criminals released
from jail, updating criminal records, inter-state co-ordination and information sharing,
effective use of MCOCA and Externment Provisions.
(iii) High visibility and presence through Group patrolling inter-alia  covers motor-cycles,
PCR vans and highway patrolling by special teams.

3.0 Safety of Senior Citizens, Juveniles and Children
3.1 Some people have suggested to the Committee that meetings with senior citizens should be
held at Thana and District levels and beat officers should regularly visit them. Participation of the
youth should be encouraged through schools and colleges. Safety of senior citizens, women and
children needs to be emphasized. Special juvenile police force should be appointed. There should
be computerization of data of missing children and linkage between district child protection unit and
district level Special Juvenile Police Unit.
3.1.1 The Committee was given to understand that senior citizens, disabled persons, children, are
the vulnerable sections of the society. Senior citizens are quite often killed sometimes by the
domestic help or by criminals. Children especially the child labourers face multi-dimensional
problems. The Committee raised the issue of safety of senior citizen, disabled, and children and
desired to know the steps taken to check crime against senior citizens and children.
3.1.2 Delhi Police informed that as a law enforcing agency committed towards securing a safe
and secure society for the common citizens and especially for the vulnerable sections like senior
citizens, Delhi Police has taken a number of initiatives in this direction. The details of specific steps
taken, apart from the usual security measures, are as follows:–
(i) Creation of Senior Citizens Security Cell  :– To co-ordinate, supervise and monitor the
efforts made by the police and different sections of society and organizations, a Senior Citizens
Security Cell was set up in Police Headquarters in June, 2004, which is presently working under
the supervision of Jt. CP/Crime. Apart from this Senior Citizens Security Cells have also been
created in all the eleven (11) police districts of Delhi.
(ii) Help Line  :– There is a Toll Free Senior Citizens Help Line No. 1291 apart from Police
Control Room no. 100, which is given wide publicity through media as well as through local police
station staff so that the senior citizens could seek prompt police help in case of any kind of
distress. The staff deputed on the helpline is regularly sensitized about the problems of the senior
citizens. The feedback of effectiveness of police action and the extent of satisfaction of senior
citizen is taken in each case and proper redressal of the grievances of senior citizens is ensured.
184 distress calls were received in 2012.
(iii) Identification and Registeration of Senior Citizens :– Senior citizens, who are living
alone or with spouse and are willing to register themselves with Delhi Police are identified by Beat/
Division staff of Police Stations and their names are forwarded to Senior Citizens Security Cell,
PHQ for registration. Senior citizens are being identified and registered with Delhi Police also
through special drives launched from time to time.
(iv) Issue of Identity Cards :– As a new initiative, Delhi Police has recently started issuing
Identity Cards to registered senior citizens which has personal particulars of the senior citizen
alongwith details of illness etc. 12812 senior citizens have been issued Identity Cards till
31.12.2012.

3.1.3 The Committee is of the considered view that senior citizens are the pillars and old
guards of the society still contributing a lot to the society and they should be respected,
admired and protected at all cost. The Committee, while noting the elaborate arrangements
undertaken by Delhi Police for protection of senior citizens, expresses its deep concern over
the cases of killings of senior citizens either by domestic help or close relatives or other
criminals with the motive to rob the property earned by them in their whole life or for any
other ulterior motive inspite of the steps taken by the Delhi Police. The Committee is of
the considered view that Delhi Police should underline the need for enforcing the preventive
measure to check crimes against senior citizens, children and women. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that Delhi Police should review and revamp its senior citizens cell.
The Committee also recommends that the security audit of all the senior citizens residing
alone in the capital may be completed in a time bound manner and representatives of the
resident’s welfare associations of the colonies/localities should also be involved in regular
meetings of Police officers.
