serious rethink on the policy. The Committee in this connection would like to suggest that
the demand of certain organizations that building reconstruction grant should not be a static
quantity and it should be on actual cost of construction and should vary from case to case

few components of the Package which have been availed could be made more attractive.

The Committee welcomes the idea of creating cluster accommodations for the
Migrants in different districts. Keeping in mind the fact that the PM’s package in the

accommodation can fulfill the twin needs of the Migrants: (i) returning to their native

Construction of Additional Two-Room Tenements at Jammu
The Committee is of the opinion that since the number of families that have shown
interest in returning to the Valley in present circumstances has remained negligible, the
demand for construction of additional two-room tenements at Jammu may be looked into
if a substantial number of families are interested in staying at Jammu so that the
rehabilitation process could be taken forward in due course of time. (Para 2.1.117)

The Committee is of the opinion that while there are no free lunches, and all

The Committee recommends that the State Government should look into the
feasibility of setting up of Notified Area Committee for providing civic amenities in Jagti.

The Committee recommends that the medical facilities in the upcoming hospital may
be started as soon as possible so that the hardships faced by the residents are mitigated.

Improvement of Living Conditions in Transit Accommodation in the Valley

by the Central Government as well as State Government of J&K. The Committee
hopes that its suggestion will be taken in right perspective with positive approach.

3.1 The Chairman, thereafter, invited the representative of Terrorism Victims/Migrants of Jammu
region and asked them to apprise the Committee about the problems being faced by migrants of
Jammu and Kashmir as well as the package announced by the Prime Minister and its
implementation. He made them acquainted about the confidentiality of the proceedings of the
Committee till the Report is submitted to Parliament.
3.2 The representative of Terrorism Affected People’s Front apprised the Committee that his
association was a constituent of Tahreek-e-Insaaf. He further made the following submissions:-
(i) J&K consists of two provinces - Jammu Province has 10 Administrative Districts while
Kashmir Province including the Ladakh area contains 12 Administrative Districts.
Terrorism erupted in 1992 in Jammu province wherein eight districts, namely Kishtwar,

56
Ramban, Doda, Riyasi, Udhampur, Kathua, Punch and Rajouri were badly affected due
to massacres.
(ii) Most of the rehabilitation programmes and development activities were concentrated in
valley areas and people of Jammu province felt neglected. According to him,
Government figures indicated that during a period of ten years from 5
th January, 1996
to 1 st May, 2006, 30 massacres occurred in Jammu province wherein 403 innocent
people were killed while in valley nine massacres took place wherein 188 civilians were
killed. Despite the fact that Jammu province was worsely affected, the province
remained deprived of development package.
(iii) There had been large scale exodus with increasing terrorism which aimed at compelling
the minority community to migrate from the area. About 12000 families were affected
in Jammu province. Since literacy rate was very low, the main source of livelihood of
the people was collection of fire wood, forest products like Bunafsa and Black
Mushroom from hilly forests. Y outh persons used to do labour work in forests. Now
all the people are deprived of the sources and people are forced to flee at the time of
harvesting. A special rehabilitation and development package at par with the Kashmiri
migrants should be given. The Supreme Court had given a ruling to give relief to
migrants of Jammu region at par with Kashmiri migrants but the State Government had
not implemented it. Besides, special recruitment drive on the lines of recruitment drive
launched for the youths of Kashmir region, should also be undertaken.
(iv) Not only Hindus, Muslims had also migrated due to frivolous complaints of supporting
terrorism and subsequent interrogations by forces. Those persons who have settled in
towns in Jammu region by getting constructed small house are not being registered for
relief as the State Government views their migration voluntary. Those migrants
numbering about 12000 should be registered and given relief.
(v) About 400 SPOs and 147 persons of Village Defence Committees had been killed. The
Government intends to disband the VDCs, while VDCs had been helpful. SPOs are paid
only R3500, hence honorarium to them needs to be enhanced. VDCs members in
Doda, Bhandarwah and Kistwar are paid but VDC members in Rajouri and Poonch are
paid nothing.
(vi) Dependants of the killed persons numbering about 1000, in Jammu Region face severe
difficulties in getting jobs on compassionate ground and their files are gethering dust
at diffetent levels and the affected persons have to go from post to pillers to complete
the formalities. The procedure in this regard should be simplified. Ex-gratia payment
of one lakh rupees only to the family of killed person is also not sufficient.
(vii) People are interested in returning to their home villages, but their properties have been
occupied by other persons.
3.3. The representatives of West Pakistan Refugees  submitted the following:
● There were about 21 thousand families consisting of fourth generation in three districts
of the State and they have no voting rights for Assembly and Panchayat elections since
independence in 1947, though they can vote in Parliamentary elections. They came to
India in 1947 even before enforcement of Article 370 and were asked to remain in the
Border Villages on the advice of Jawahar Lal Nehru and Sheikh Abdullah. However,
they are not considered eligible for Government jobs, even under the Central
Government as the jobs are made in the name of State Government, which did not
treat them state subjects. In the recruitments for army and para military forces,

57
domicile certificates are asked, which they do not have. People are living at the land
which was given by compassionate basis. However, they are now not permitted to get
repaired the diapilated houses. They are not getting benefits under Indira Awas Yojana
and Anganwadi schemes.
● Majority of families belong to Scheduled Caste, but the constitutional benefits are being
denied to them. State Government has stopped issuing SC and OBC certificates to
them and children are facing difficulties in getting admissions in the schools and
colleges. PM package is not being implemented and correspondence with the State
Government has not yielded any result.
● They should be given voting rights so that their generations can live properly and if
it is not possible, they may be rehabilitated somewhere else in the vast country.
3.4 The representatives of the Pakistan Occupied Jammu Kashmir Refugees mentioned
that PoK’ is a misnomer and It should be ‘PoJK’ as it has very less part namely Muzzarafabad
of Kashmir; Gilgit, Baltistan formed apart of Leh-Laddakh. At the time of partition, migrated people
from Muzzarafabad and Poonch were not allowed to stay in Kashmir and were directed to go to
Jammu. They were told that after resolving of PoK issues, they would be sent back. They however
have voting rights and eligible for Government jobs. In 1960 they were given relief of
R3500 however R2500 were deducted in lieu of land provided. The relief was given subject to the
conditions i.e. (i) person must be staying in the camps not with relatives (ii) head of the family
also should have migrated and (iii) migration should be within September, 1947 and December,
1950. Families whose head of the family was killed during migration and migrated after December,
1950 were left. The Petitions Committee of Rajya Sabha in 32
nd Report recommended for
rehabilitation and compensation, which was not implemented. Recommendations of the Wadhwa
Committee set up by the State Government in 2007 were also not implemented.

● The migrants should be registered. 31600 families were registered while 9500 families
were not registered as they could not fulfill the condition. The properties which were
lost have not been compensated. One third of the population of POJK migrated to
Jammu. They should be provided with political rights in exile as they spread to the

courses.
● Refugee Development Board should be constituted to look after the development needs
of such migrants. Out of the ex-gratia payment of 3500 rupees 2500 was deducted
against provision of land which was never given even after 65 years. Now the
Government is giving 1,50,000 rupees on account of non-grant of land promised.

REPORT 
I, the Chairman, Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee, present this Eighteenth Report relating to the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, 
1995•. The Bill seeks to make special provisions for the prevention of, and for coping with 
terrorist and disruptive activities and to supplement the criminal law. 
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred .. the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya 
Sabha on the 18th May, 1995 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and 
report within two days. 
3. Accordingly, the Committee considered the Bill in its meeting held on the 19th May, 
1995 and also heard the Home Secretary. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the report in its meeting held on the 22nd 
May, 1995. 
5. Some Members of the Committee gave amendments/suggestions on the Bill which 
are appended to the report. 
6. In his presentation, the Home Secretary stated that the following provisions under 
TADA which were either misused or had the potential of being misused are proposed to be 
dropped in the new legislation:-
(i) Section 5 of TADA Act makes unauthorised possession~f arms in a notified area 
an offence. The Arms Act provides for deterrent punishment for possession of 
certain classes of unauthorised arms. Therefore, there is no need to repeat the 
provision in the new legislation. 
(ii) Section 15 of T ADA Act provides that confessions made to a police officer are 
admissible in evidence. This is against the grain of the normal provision of the 
Indian Evidence Act, 1872 whereunder statements made to the police are not 
admissible as evidence. 
(iii) Section 21(1)(c) and (d) lays down certain presumptions relating to confessions. 
This section provides that if it is proved that one of the accused makes a confession 
that the other has committed the offence, it shall be presumed that the other 
(accused) has committed the offence. It also provides that if it is proved that an 
accused has made a confession to any person other than a police officer, it shall be 
presumed that he has committed such an offence. 
(iv) Section 20(8)(b) provides that a court shall not grant bail unless it is satisfied that 
•Published in the Gazette of India, Extraordinary Part-11, Section 2, dated the 18th May, 1995. 
**Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part-II, dated the 18th May, 1995. 

there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty Of an 
offence under T ADA. This provision made it extremely difficult to obtain bail in 
TADA cases. 
The Home Secretary also enumerated the following safeguards in the proposed 
legislation to check its abuse:-
(i) Presently under TADA Act an appeal from the designated court lies to the 
Supreme Court. It has been argued that under Indian conditions , with prevailing 
poverty, it is difficult for poor people to approach straightaway the Supreme Court . 
In the new legislation, an appeal has, therefore, been provided to the High Court . 
(ii) As suggested by the Supreme Court, a provision has been made -that investigation 
in the cases relating to terrorist and disruptive activities should be done by an 
officer not below in rank than that of a Deputy Superintendent of Police. This 
would cut down the misuse substantially. 
(iii) A provision has been made that for vexatious , malicious or corrupt actions by the 
police whereby any person is wrongly arrested or threatened to be arrested , are 
made punishable with an imprisonment upto one year or with fine, or with both. 
(iv) In a normal case any police officer can 1egister a case, make an investigation , and 
file charge-sheet . But, in the new legislation there are three stages. Firstly, no 
information about the commission of an offence shall be recorded by the police 
without the prior approval of the District Superintendent of Police . Secondly , the 
investigation of an offence shall not be done by a police officer below the rank of 
Deputy Superintendent of Police/ Assistant Commissioner of Police. Thirdly , no 
court shall take cognizance of an offence under this new legislation without the 
previous sanction of Inspector-General of Police/Commissioner of Police . 
7. Among the salient feature s of the present Bill, the Home Secretary mentioned the 
setting up of the Special Courts for speedy disposal of the cases, because if the cases relating 
to terrorism are also to be dealt with by the ordinary courts , it woufd take years together 
•before the case would come up for hearing or it may not come up for hearing at all. 
Secondly , the police custody is for thirty days as against sixty days under the TADA Act . 
The judicial custody which was earlier one year (six months divided into two parts) has been 
reduced to six months (in two parts of three months each). If the investigations are not 
completed within this period; the court has to be approached again. 
8. Several Members were of the view that the opposition to TADA today is based on 
thousands of T ADA cases made out against thousands of innocent persons and that the new 
legislation does not provide any relief to these! persons. The Home Secretary clarified that a 
criminal law had always prospective effect and not -applied retrospectively . The proposed 
legislation would come into force after it becomes an Act of Parliament and would apply to 
the offences committed thereafter. He further added that in respect of the old TADA cases, 
there_ is already a provision in sub-section (4) of section 1 of the TADA Act , according to 
which the old cases would continue ~o be dealt with as per the existing law of the land. The 
Home Secretary, however, apprised the Committee that the cases of T ADA detenues are 
being reviewed administratively at the Central and the State level as per the direction of the 
Supreme Court. Under this direction, high level administrative committees are to be 
constituted. At the Central level, the Committee is headed by the Home Secretary, and the 
Law Secretary and the Director, CBI as its members. At the State level, these Committees 
would consist of the Home Secretary, the Law Secretary and the Director-General of Police . 
In some cases, these Committees are beaded by Retd. High Court Judges. These 

Committees review the cases to see whether the T ADA provisions have been applied 
properly or not. As a result of this system of review, thousands of cases have been 
cancelled/withdrawn/filedlfADA provisions dropped benefiting a very large number of 
persons. In this context, the Home Secretary stated that these review Committees were 
being made more powerful and vigorous and they were also meeting regularly. 
9. In reply to another query regarding the need for statutory review Committee in the 
Bill, as in the case of National Security Act, Maintenance of Internal Security Act etc., the 
Home Secretary clarified that under the National Security Act and other preventive 
detention laws, there is no court and there is no trial. The detenue does not go to the court 
and the court has only wni jurisdiction. But in the present case a charge-sheet is filed, trial 
takes place and the court decide the case. The idea of statutory review C~mmittee would, 
therefore, be meaningless. So, there is a wide difference between the two. It is for this 
reason that the Supreme Court has observed that as regards pending T ADA cases, these 
should be admin'istratively reviewed. 
10. Some Members expressed the appreh&nsion that the new legislation might be 
misused against political opponents, trade unionists and workers. They were of the firm view 
that adequate safeguards should be there in the proposed fegislation to check its misuse. In 
reply to a quer y whether the proposed legislation has been brought after consulting the 
Chief Ministers, the Home Secretary stated that discussions had taken place with them and 
their views had been ascertained and the Bill has been prepared reflecting their views. 
11. Prior to considering this Bill, the Committee had occasion to discuss the TADA in 
its meetings held on the 4th and lOth May, 1995 and hear the Home Secretary in the matter. 
After deliberations, the general view which emerged in the Committee was that the T ADA 
Act should be repealed and either a separate legislation should be enacted to counter 
terrorism or the essential legal requirements to fight terrorism be incorporated in the normal 
laws of the land, with in-built safequards against misuse. The view of the Committee and the 
connected papers were forwarded to the Government for consideration. 
12. In view of the above and after hearing the Home Secretary and taking into 
consideration the views expressed by the Members on 19th May, 1995 the following views 
emerged while adopting the Report on the Bill on 22nd May, 1995:-
- The present bill was uot necessary as the existing laws of the land were adequate to 
curb the menace of the terrorism. 
- The bill in necessary to counter terrorism and disruptive activities. 
- The bill should be criculated to all Chief Ministers for their views and public opinion 
should also be elicited. 
- The present law should not be a permanent statute and should be periodically 
reviewed after every three years. 
- Compensation should be given to innocent victims of the TADA. 
- The direction of the Supreme Court regarding Review Committees should be made a 
part of the new legislation. 
- An integrated view should be taken of the whole situation and that the existing Jaws 
such as N.S.A., D.I.R etc. were quite adequate to meet the problem of terrorism 
and disruptive activities. So, there was no need to incorporate some of the· provisions 
of the T ADA in the new legislation. 
- The definitions in the new .legislation should be modified and made specific to check 
its misuse. 

In the light of the suggestions, views, observations and amendments made by the 
members, the Committee adopts this Report on the Bill for consideration of the House.

Dear Sir, 
I propose the following amendments to the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, 1995:-
1. The Criminal Law Amendment Bill, 1995 seeks to replace the 10 year old Terrorist 
and Disruptive Activities (prevention) Act (TADA). Even though TADA was 
draconian the saving grace was that it was time-bound, unlike the present Bill which 
would become a permanent law in our statute book. There is no need for making 
this law as perpetual. I suggest three-year time limit for the operation of the law 
after which it may be reviewed according to the needs of the times. 
2. Oauses 3 and 4 define terrorism and disruptive activities. These definitions are not 
precise but nebulous and capable of misuse. Clause 3 contains .15 independent 
offences. It is nothing but rearrangement of offences against the State as enumerated 
in Macaulay's Penal Code. This clause should be made precise so as to exclude trade 
union activities and political activities like peaceful 'hartal' etc. Otherwise a country 
made bomb or a gelatine stick can easily be planted and false charges may be cooked 
up. 
3. Oause 4 deals with disruptive activity. It enumerates several independent offences 
and is a mere restatement of provisions dealing with the public tranquility in the 
Indian Penal Code. We find in some of these provisions the Kafkaesque dimensions. 
For instance under sub clause (3) of clause 4 'prophecy' 'prediction' 'pronouncement' 
have been made offences. The astrologers and god-men that the members of the 
Cabinet at Delhi frequent may qualify for being contingent terrorists should the~ 
dilate on their longevity. 
4. Oause 8(7) says the judge or the additional judge of the Special Court may continut 
in service even after superannuation i.e. until the case is over. This will give place t1 
picking up of selective judges and therefore this provision should be deleted. 
5. Oause 14 provides for keeping the identity and address of a witness as secret an 
permits avoidance of their names and addresses in the Special C'...ourt's orders c 
judgements or in any records of the case accessible in public. Probably it is due t 
the apprehension that the said witness may be harmed. Yet, it is not fair. TI 
identity should be known to the accu&ed and cross-examination of the witness is 
must for any fair trial. Therefore, this obnoxious provision ~ould be deleted. 
6. Clause 18(2) :xtends the remand period. One of the factors that caused the misuse 
T ADA was the difficulty in getting the bail for the accused. The present provisi• 
may likewise tempt the authorities to misuse the said Act and therefore I comme 
for its deletion.

THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT BILL, 1995 
NOTE 
The Criminal Law Amendment Bill, 1995 has been introduced on 18th May, 1995 in the 
Rajya Sabha. In the Statement of Objects and Reasons (Para 4) given for the present Bill, it 
has been mentioned that Chief Ministers and Governors of States have been consulted "and 
in the light of views expressed by the Chief Ministers and Governors as also the Leaders of 
various political parties, the Government have decided not to extend the life of the Terrorist 
and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act." This seems to be far from the truth. The 
consensus in the Chief Ministers' Conference was in favour of the retention of the TADA 
Act with some modifications to provide safeguards against its possible misuse. 
Section 17 - Bail 
The provisions for granting bail have now been diluted to the extent that even hardened 
terrorists would be able to get bail easily. This will have serious repercussions particularly in 
J & K where terrorism is at its extreme. Under the T ADA, an appeal from the designated 
court lies with the Supreme Court. This should continue. 
Section 24(2) - Punishment of Police Officials 
Under the proposed sub-section (2) of Section 24, punishment of imprisonment upto J 
year has been provided for policemen or corruptly or maliciously proceed or threaten t< 
proceed against any person for an offence under the new Jaw. This provision of actim 
against policemen would totally demoralise the police force and no police officer would lik• 
to proceed under the new law for fear of prosecution. When the proposed law alread 
provides for registration. of a case with the approval of the SP and launching of prosecutio 
only with the sanction of the IG, Police, there is no need at all to provide for prosecution c 
policemen. Hence, this sub-section should be deleted. 
Strengthening the Bill 
As pointed out above, the Criminal Law Amendment Bill as it has been drafted seen 
to have no teeth to deal with the threat of terrorism and disruptive elements. The curre· 
situation in the country requires a stringent law to deal with the anti-national elemen 
seeking to spread terrorism in the country. The proposed law would be ineffective in dealiJ 
with the menace of terrorism.

CHAPTER-I
DADRA AND NAGAR HA VELI
1.1 INTRODUCTION
1.1.1 Dadra and Nagar Haveli was born on 17 th December, 1779 as a result of a treaty between
Portuguese and Marathas. The Marathas assigned 72 villages to Portuguese in return of their
friendship and the group of 72 villages came to be known as Dadra and Nagar Haveli. The
Portuguese ruled this territory until its liberation on 2
nd August, 1954. After its liberation, the
Administration was carried on by local body known as Free Dadra and Nagar Haveli Administration
till its merger with the Indian Union on 11
th August, 1961. Consequently, the Free Dadra and Nagar
Haveli Administration was succeeded by formal statutory Administration headed by an Administrator.
1.1.2 This UT has an area of 491 sq.km. and comprises of two enclaves viz. (1) Dadra and
(2) Nagar Haveli. Five villages in the UT viz. Dadra, Naroli, Samarvarni, Masat and Rakholi are
treated as statutory Census Towns in population Census 2011. Besides, this UT has 65 villages, one
District Panchayat, 11 Village Panchayats and one Municipal Council. Silvasa is the capital city of
this UT.

1.4 ISSUES PERTAINING TO INDUSTRIES
1.4.1 The Sub-Committee during its study visit interacted with representatives of trade and
industry associations and Trade Union and other Associations of UTs of Daman and Diu and Dadra
and Nagar Haveli at Silvassa. During the interaction, following issues emerged before the Sub-
Committee:–
Tax Exemption
1.4.2 According to the UT administration, Dadra and Nagar Haveli is predominantly a backward
area both economically as well as industrially. After liberation from Portuguese regime in 1954 and
merger with the Union of India in 1962, the industrial development made a low key start in the
year 1965 by establishing a industrial estate under co-operative sector namely Dan Udyog Sahakari
Sangh Ltd.
1.4.3 The Sub-Committee was informed that in the beginning there was no sales tax leviable as
it was backward territory inhabited by Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. However, with the
increase in Industries, trade and commercial activities in the U.T., there was persistence from the
neighbouring States to discontinue the exemption of tax to avoid unhealthy competition of prices
among the neighboring States; it was decided to impose sales tax in the UT of Dadra and Nagar
Haveli. Thus, Sales Tax regime came into force from 1983 and the Industrial Units who so ever
established were eligible for sales tax exemption for the period of 15 years. This Scheme was in
force upto 1998. At present the newly established Units are getting the benefit of Central Sales Tax
exemption which is available upto the year 2017.
1.4.4 Further with the implementation of V AT Policy at all India level, the Dadra and Nagar Haveli
Regulation 2005 and Dadra and Nagar Haveli Value Added Rules 2005 were enforced with effect
from 01.04.2005. Thus at present following tax laws are in force.

8
● The Central Sales Tax Act, 1956
● The Central Sales Tax (Dadra and Nagar Haveli) Rules, 1983
● The Dadra and Nagar Haveli Value Added Tax Regulation, 2005
1.4.5 It was further informed that w.e.f. 1 st April 1993, 100% deduction is available to the
Industrial establishments in their profit and gains, for the 1st five years and the same were available
up to March, 2002 implying that those units which began to manufacture or produce articles on
or before 30th March, 2002 were entitled for 100% income tax holiday for the 1st five assessment
years. Also after the initial five years benefit, such industrial undertakings are entitled to the
deduction at the rate of 25% for their profits and gains for the next five assessment years.
1.4.6 The industry associations of the Dadra and Nagar Haveli submitted a representation before
the Sub-Committee with a request to take up the issue of tax-exemption. Responding to
the request, the Ministry informed that Tax benefit is available in the U.T. of DNH upto
31st December, 2017 and Proposal for extension of benefits received from the UT Administration
vide its letter dated 30th November, 2013 is under consideration in the Ministry.
1.4.7 The Committee takes note of the submission of the UT Administration that they
have requested the Ministry for further extension of tax benefits. The Committee
understands that due to the exemption of V AT, many big industries have set up plants in
this Union Territory leading to development in the Union Territory. The Committee

CHAPTER-II
DAMAN AND DIU
2.1 INTRODUCTION
2.1.1 For over 450 years, the coastal enclaves of Daman and Diu on the Arabian Sea coast were
part of Portuguese India, along with Goa and Dadra and Nagar Haveli. Goa, Daman and Diu were
incorporated into the Republic of India on 19 th December, 1961 by military conquest. Portugal did
not recognize the Indian annexation of these territories until 1974. The territory of “Goa, Daman
and Diu” was administered as a single Union Territory until 30
th May, 1987, when Goa was granted
statehood, leaving Daman and Diu as a separate Union Territory.
2.1.2 Daman is on main land on sea-shore near southern portion of Gujarat State. Diu is an island
near Una Taluka of Junagarh District in Gujarat State. For administration purposes, there are two
Districts namely, Daman and Diu, two tehsils, two blocks, two towns, fourteen Village Panchayats
and twenty six villages in the UT with Daman as the Head Quarter of the UT with 100% of grant
from the Government of India in the form of Central assistance.
2.1.3 There is one parliamentary constituency and one District Panchayat in the UT. The
Committee was informed that Daman and Diu has the oldest history of urbanization as it has oldest
Urban Local Bodies viz. Municipal Councils. The total population of the UT is 2,42,911 with
Literacy rate at 91.48 per cent. The UT has total urban area of 24.26 sq. kms. with 36.25% of
the total population. There are two Municipal Councils one at Daman and the other at Diu. UT of
Daman and Diu does not have its own power generation. 93% of the electricity is consumed by
Industries. JERC determines the tariff for all classes of consumers.

CHAPTER-III
CHANDIGARH
3.1 INTRODUCTION
3.1.1 Chandigarh city recognized as the well planned, maintained, cleanest and greenest city of
the country is one of the best experiments in urban planning and modern architecture in the
twentieth century in India. Chandigarh derives its name from the temple of “Chandi Mandir” located
in the vicinity of the site selected for the city.
3.1.2 Since the medieval period through modern era of Indian history, the area was part of the
large Punjab Province which was divided into East and West Punjab during partition of the country
in 1947. The city was conceived to be made the capital of East Punjab and to resettle West Punjab
refugees coming from Pakistan. In 1948, Punjab Government, in consultation with the Government
of India, approved the area of the foothills of the Shivaliks as the site for the new capital. The
location of the city site was a part of the erstwhile Ambala district. The foundation stone of the
city was laid in 1952. Subsequently, at the time of reorganization of the State in 1966 into Punjab,
Haryana and Himachal Pradesh, this city was made the capital of both, Punjab and Haryana and
was declared as a Union Territory in the direct control of the Central Government.
3.1.3 After reorganization of Punjab in 1966, the Administration of the UT was under the Chief
Commissioner. From 1
st June, 1984, the Governor of Punjab took over the direct Administration of
the UT and the post of Chief Commissioner was re-designed as Adviser to the Administrator. The
Union Territory Administration is headed by the Administrator who is appointed by the President
of India under Article 239(2) of the Constitution of India. The Administrator is assisted by the
Adviser to the Administrator who usually happens to be an IAS officer of the AGMU cadre. The
Administration of Chandigarh follows the Punjab Municipal Corporation Law (Extension to
Chandigarh) Act, 1976 following which the Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh came into
existence in May, 1994.
3.1.4 The master plan of Chandigarh was prepared by the French architect Le Corbusier as
analogous to human body, with a clearly defined head (the Capitol Complex, Sector 1), heart (the
City Centre Sector-17), lungs (the leisure valley, innumerable open spaces and sector greens), the
intellect (the cultural and educational institutions), the circulatory system (the network of roads, the
7Vs) and the viscera (the Industrial Area). The concept of the city is based on four major
functions: living, working, care of the body and spirit and circulation. Residential sectors constitute
the living part whereas the Capitol Complex, City Centre, Educational Zone (Post Graduate Institute,
Punjab Engineering College, Punjab University) and the Industrial Area constitute the working part.
The Leisure Valley, Gardens, Sector Greens and Open Courtyards etc. are for the care of body and
spirit. The circulation system comprises of 7 different types of roads known as 7Vs. Later on, a
pathway for cyclists called V8 was added to this circulation system. Tree plantation and
landscaping has been an integral part of the city master plan. Different types of flowering and
various species of evergreen have been planted along the roads, in parking areas, shopping
complexes, residential areas and in the city parks.
3.1.5 According to UT Administration, Chandigarh was planned for a population of half-a-million.
In Phase I, 36 sq. km. of land was acquired by the city administration for construction of
25

26
30 sectors. Land for seventeen additional sectors (Sector 31 to 47) was acquired and developed
during the second phase to cater for a population of 350,000. The predominance of multistoried
apartments in the second phase provide for higher population dimension. However, Chandigarh has
now grown beyond its planned capacity. Hence, development in the third phase has started in
Sectors 48 and beyond. By 2021 the population of Chandigarh is projected to be around 19.5 lacs
(at current rate of growth) almost four times for which it was originally built.

3.2 PROJECT/SCHEMES

Smart School
3.2.5 The Sub-Committee visited a Smart school of UT of Chandigarh. This smart school in the
UT of Chandigarh has led to the classroom teaching going beyond the confines of text-books. The
Chandigarh Administration has conceptualized such schools with the objective of making learning
an enjoyable experience, integrating students with society and preparing them for future challenges,
developed a visionary plan for the roll out of ‘smart school concept.
3.2.6 According to the UT Administration, the educational content in smart school solution is
strictly mapped to NCERT books and can be easily customized to any State boards. In these
schools, emphasis has been given on the use of information and communication technology. The
class rooms in such schools are proposed to be equipped with Plasma Screens and other
peripherals. All educational services of the school will be interconnected and centralized with the
Principal, who will act as Nodal Officer for all the activities.
3.2.7 The Committee understands that in this electronic age, integrated e-teaching and
learning methodologies in our schools have become imperative and through establishing
smart schools, UT Government can fulfill goals of bridging digital divide and empowering the
future generation of the country. The Committee appreciates the modernization process of
schooling system with emphasis on interactive boards, multimedia and maximum use of
e-contents. The Committee hopes that these smart schools will go a long way in terms of
achieving excellence in academics, co-curricular area and the educational management. The
Committee recommends that more and more schools with such facilities should be set up
in the UT and existing schools should be converted into smart ones. This project should also
be implemented in other UTs and States should also be advised to embrace technology in
class rooms by setting up of smart schools.

Rajiv Gandhi Chandigarh Technology Park (RGCTP)
3.2.11 The Sub-Committee visited RGCTP in the city of Chandigarh. The Sub-Committee was
informed that Rajiv Gandhi Chandigarh Technology Park (RGCTP) is an extremely important
project for the Union Territory of Chandigarh as it provides world class integrated infrastructure
necessary for the setting up of facilities/campuses by leading technology companies and other IT/
ITES/BPO companies for the first time in this region. Chandigarh has traditionally been a city
where not many multi-national companies had earlier set up their facilities and therefore a large
number of professionals had left Chandigarh in the past for other cities, in search of high level
employment. The level of educational facilities here had been much higher than the level of
employment opportunities available, especially in the knowledge sector and RGCTP is a major step
in the direction of plugging this gap.
3.2.12 According to UT Administration, the vision was to establish a world class IT Park with
state of the art infrastructure including the provision of 100% availability of power and broadband
connectivity. As the Tier I cities like Bangalore, Hyderabad, NCR of Delhi were getting choked
because of the IT boom in India, meticulous planning and aggressive marketing of Chandigarh as
an IT destination placed Chandigarh on the national map as an excellent Tier II destination which
started attracting the attention of a lot of IT multinational companies. As such, huge demand of
IT space started pouring in and the area of 123 acres started looking small.
3.2.13 According to UT Administration, the development of RGCTP has been anchored by
Infosys, which has completed its state of the art campus. DLF is also offering ready to use built
up space and is already housing 37 IT Companies. These state of the art buildings are already
providing directly employment to more than 6000 professionals. IT majors like Wipro, Bharti Airtel,
Tech Mahindra, alongwith 21 other companies are in the process of developing their respective
sites allotted to them.
3.2.14 Apart from a Hotel cum Convention Centre, a T ech Habitat Centre is also under
development on a 123 acre plot under PPP model. This project has been planned taking into
consideration the logistic needs relating to the residential accommodation for the IT professionals
who would be working in RGCTP.
3.2.15 Keeping in view the pending applications for various sizes of plots in RGCTP and the huge
demand pouring in from various quarters across the globe, another 272 acres of land have been
planned for expansion of RGCTP. The land for this Phase is under acquisition, which is likely to
be completed shortly, after which further allotments will be undertaken as per the Policy.
3.2.16 The Committee hopes that world class integrated infrastructure for the setting up
of facilities/campuses by leading Technology Companies and other IT/ITES/BPO companies
for the first time in this region will help increasing employment generation for IT
professionals as well as development of information technology infrastructure in the UT. The
Committee recommends that acquisition of another 272 acres of land for further expansion

enhance exports from the city.

been built. The Committee hopes that this Centre will help enhance export of the software
products from the UT and assist young professionals in setting up their entrepreneurship.

up export oriented units in the EDC.

3.4 MUNICIPAL CORPORATION OF CHANDIGARH
3.4.1 During the visit of the Sub-Committee, the Commissioner, Municipal Corporation of
Chandigarh also made a presentation before the Sub-Committee on 27
th July, 2012. According to
the Commissioner out of total area of 114 sq. km. of Chandigarh, the total area coming under the
jurisdiction of Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh is 79.34 sq. km. The Municipal area has
population of 9.44 lakh out of total population of 10.54 lakh. The entire area of Municipal
Corporation has been divided into 26 wards and each ward is represented by an elected councilor.
Besides, 9 members from amongst the persons, who are eminent/distinguished in public affairs, are
nominated by the Administrator, U.T. Chandigarh. The Member of Parliament from Chandigarh is
an ex-officio member. One third of total number of seats to be filled up by direct election is
reserved for women. Similarly, out of seats reserved for scheduled castes, one third seats are
reserved for women belonging to Scheduled Castes. Mayor is the Head of Elected Body assisted
by Sr. Deputy Mayor and Deputy Mayor. Obligatory and discretionary functions of the Corporation
are enshrined in Section 44 and 45 of the Municipal Act. Water supply and sewerage, storm water
drainage, street lighting, sanitation, community centres, roads and bridges, horticulture, fire
services, registration of births and deaths, primary health and primary education are major
functions entrusted to Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh.
3.4.2 The working of Municipal Corporation is based on the committee system under which
various Sub-Committees dealing with specified subjects, such as Finance and Contract, Water
supply and Sewerage disposal, Road, House Tax Assessment, Electricity, Environment and City
Beautification, Sanitation, Day Market and Apni Mandi, Fire and Emergency Services, Enforcement,
Arts Culture and Sports, Slum Colonies and Village Development exist. They are headed by a
Chairman whereas the Finance and Contract Committee is headed by Mayor. The financial power
of Finance and Contract Committee is upto R35 lakh. The tenure of these Committees is one year.
Different Committees have been delegated financial and other powers to carry on the functions
relating to Municipal Corporation. The matter involving financial implication beyond
R35 lakh and policy decisions are placed before the General body (House) meeting of the
Corporation.
3.4.3 The UT Administration was asked about steps required to further strengthen the working
of Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh. The UT Administration submitted that since its inception
various functions/departments have been transferred to Municipal Corporation in a phased manner,
as a result of which the responsibilities of the Corporation have been increased considerably.
Therefore, it requires strengthening of the Corporation by taking following steps:–
● Strengthening of manpower
● Strengthening of infrastructure/machinery
● Strengthening of MCC using Information Technology
● Increase in Annual Budget.

31
3.4.4 The UT Administration was asked whether allocated budgetary provisions are sufficient for
carrying out the development projects. In its response, it was stated that the allocated budgetary
provision is insufficient for carrying out the development projects. About 10.83% of the budget
(Plan and Non Plan) of Chandigarh is allocated to MCC. 17.5% of the Tax Revenue of
Administration is paid on Grant-in-Aid to the MCC as per the recommendations of 3rd Delhi
Finance Commission.
3.4.5 On the question of criteria for devolution of funds to the Local Bodies keeping in view the
increasing functions and jurisdiction of Municipal Corporation, Chandigarh, the UT Administration
stated that no criteria for devolution of funds to the Local Bodies has been conveyed to the
Chandigarh Administration by the Government of India. However, Chandigarh Administration is
providing financial aid to Municipal Corporation, Chandigarh on account of developmental works
from the Plan budget in addition to Government of India Grant being paid as per the
recommendations of 3rd Delhi Finance Commission.
3.4.6 The UT Administration was asked whether it is being contemplated to increase the revenue
of Municipal Corporation as the Corporation has more responsibility with limited authority and
financial resources. The UT Administration in its response has admitted that it is being
contemplated to increase the revenue of MC, U.T. Chandigarh. Recently, Municipal Corporation has
imposed tax on residential property @ R1/- per square yard. This will increase the revenue of the
Municipal Corporation, U.T., Chandigarh and the revision of proposed rates of Tax is under
examination of the Municipal Corporation, Chandigarh.
3.4.7 According to the UT Administration, the fourth Delhi Finance Commission has been
constituted to find out the shortcomings in the budgetary provisions. The detailed report has been
given to the Delhi Finance Commission to consider and suggest ways and means to increase the
revenue share of the Municipal Corporation, Chandigarh. The measures so suggested by the Fourth
Delhi Finance Commission shall be further examined for adoption.
3.4.8 The Committee recommends that increasing financial power of Finance and Contract
Committee of Chandigarh Municipal Corporation which is headed by Mayor upto one crore
rupees should be considered as keeping in view the municipal area of Chandigarh, 35 lakh
is meager amount.
3.4.9 The Committee also recommends that strengthening of manpower and infrastructure
of MCC is the handicap in its efficient discharge of mandate. Strengthening of MCC in
terms of using Information Technology is also required. The Committee therefore
recommends that the UT Administration should take all corrective actions proactively to
remove hurdles in the way of MCC. Besides, there should be maximum use of information
technology in the offices of Municipal body so that residents could get their work done
hassle free.
3.4.10 After going through details of budgetary provisions and expenditure during the last
five years of Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh, the Committee disapprovingly notes that
the Municipal Corporation has not been able to spend the allocated amount in any financial
year. The Committee views that the demand of the UT Administration for more money to
MCC as the allocated budgetary provision is insufficient for carrying out the development
projects is misplaced. The Committee recommends that the MCC should strive to increase
its fund absorption capacity for carrying out the development projects in the municipal area
of the UT with alacrity.

issues pertaining to the industries in Chandigarh which was forwarded to the Ministry for replies/

“the plots/sheds shall hence-forth be allotted to Industrial houses for promotion of

notified shortly.

be notified. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) should
impress upon the UT administration for redrafting new industrial policy of UT in consonance
with the MSMED Act, 2006 which the Centre had formulated for the overall industrial growth

33
and accommodate the grievances of local industrialists. The UT Administration should also
invite objections/suggestions from stakeholders of the industry before finalising the policy.

tech, low-volume and high value-added industries is needed for the UT. However, interests

3.5.11 The rates were revised by way of a notification way back in 2007 and thus carry sanctity

34

3.5.23 The issues raised in the representation would be taken up with the concerned Ministry.

3.6.8 There was a demand of delinking of the inspection for building violations with/from the

Response of the Ministry
3.6.9 In response, the UT Administration has stated that there have been a lot of violations of
the existing bye laws of the Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952. According

39
to the UT Administration, a survey was conducted in 2000 wherein it was found that 75-80% of
building violations exist in the Dwelling Units of Chandigarh Housing Board. It has mentioned that

conversion letter to the applicants for executing Conveyance Deed with the Registrar, UT,
Chandigarh. When the applicant applies for transfer of ownership on the basis of GPA and Sale
Deed, the CHB as per procedure takes the building violation/misuse report. In case, there is building

now the proposal is being submitted to the Board for consideration and approval for allowing
transfer on the basis of affidavit of the applicant stating therein that there is no building violation/
misuse in the dwelling unit.
3.6.10 The UT Administration has further mentioned that the CHB is transferring the dwelling unit
on the basis of GPA/Sub-GPA, where the transaction has taken place after a lock-in period of
5 years from the date of physical possession as per provisions of the approved GPA transfer policy
under Regulation-16 of Chandigarh Housing Board (Allotment, Management and Sale of Tenements)
Regulations, 1979. In such cases, a no-violation report is presently being taken. It has also
informed that the proposal is being submitted to the Board for consideration and approval on the
basis of affidavit submitted by the applicant.
3.6.11 On the issue of delinking of the inspection for building violations from the process
of transfer of ownership by Chandigarh Housing Board Residents Federation, the Committee
is of the opinion that the issue has merit and the UT administration should reconsider its
decision in this regard.
Allowing transfer on GPA basis
3.6.12 There was a request for allowing transfer on GPA basis to the transactions within the
lock-in period of five years.
Response of the Ministry
3.6.13 The UT Administration has stated that the Dwelling Units (DUs) had been allotted by the

Attorney etc. except to surrender it to the Board during the Hire Purchase period or for a period

a tenant and he shall have no other right except those of tenancy.
3.6.14 The Regulation 16 of Chandigarh Housing Board (Allotment, Management and Sale of
Tenements) Regulations, 1979 is reproduced as under:–
“16 Transfer of Registration/property: - Notwithstanding anything contained in these
regulations, the Board may transfer the registration number or any property after a period
of 5 years from the date of physical possession by imposing such terms and conditions as

40

which are covered under the original GPA Transfer Policy framed by the Board as per terms and
conditions as laid down in the original policy. The UT Administration while further clarifying has

transfer of dwelling units has taken place after the initial lock-in-period of 5 years as specified in

43

Shortage of Drinking Water
3.7.28 The non-cooperative attitude of adjoining States of Punjab and Haryana in not allowing
water from Bhakra Canal for augmentation of water supply scheme of the city from Kaujoliwater
works has further exaggerated the problem. River water is a Natural National Resource and the
Union Government should include the water in the concurrent list to help the Centre to have a
greater say in settling such interstate disputes.

45
Response of the Ministry
3.7.29 The quantity of drinking water available to the City residents is 87 MGD which is made
available through two main sources viz. (i) from 210 deep tube wells (underground water)=20
MGD; (ii) from Bhakra Canal located 28 km. from the city (Surface water brought to city through
4 pipelines)=58 MGD; (iii) Share of Panchkula and Chandimandir of Bhakra water presently being
used by Chandigarh city=9 MGD. As per real time data available with the Municipal Corporation
through its billing, it is observed that city residents are being supplied 252 ltrs. per capita per day
(lpcd) which is much above the national norm of 135 lpcd. As such, there is no shortage of
drinking water supply in the city. To maintain adequate pressure in all the areas, 70 water boosting
stations scattered all over the city have been constructed and are in operation. These boosting
stations maintain adequate pressure in otherwise low pressure areas. During the current summer
season, the consumer satisfaction regarding supply of drinking water was found to be much higher
than the previous years due to continuous monitoring/management/ checking of leakages by the
Public Health wing of MCC. During peak summer season, the demand of drinking water rises and
estimated shortfall is 29 MGD. In order to meet this peak demand, a project to bring 40 MGD
additional water from Bhakra Main line at Kajauli got approved under JNNURM but it could not
be executed due to non availability of consent of the States of Punjab and Haryana due to their
interstate issues. However, GMADA is laying a bigger dia pipeline of capacity 80 MGD for bringing
water from Bhakra Main Line at Kajauli to Mohali and satellite towns. Efforts are being made to
persue the States of Punjab and Haryana for releasing 40 MGD for Chandigarh which can be
brought to the city through this bigger dia pipeline. Chandigarh has implemented an ambitious
project under JNNURM to supply tertiary water to all the green belts, gardens and houses having
area more than 1 kanal. The tertiary water plant along with rising main and network of pipes
supplying tertiary water to all areas of the city has since been commissioned and is in operation.
All big institutions, golf club, golf course, green belts, gardens and neighbourhood parks have been
covered with tertiary treated water. The tariff rates for supply of tertiary treated water have been
kept low by the MCC in order to promote its usages in big way so as to conserve fresh water
which otherwise is being used for irrigation by big households. Regarding recharging of water
through rain water harvesting, work has been entrusted to Centre for Science and Environment,
New Delhi for preparing a pilot project for one sector of the city. After studying the results of
this project, it can be replicated to other parts of the city.
3.7.30 The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take up this
matter at the highest level for getting water from Bhakra Canal for augmentation of
Kajouli water works. The UT administration should also promote water conservation through
rain water harvesting and ground water recharge etc. in the UT to tackle water woes and
ensure long-term sustainability of water sources for the city. A comprehensive water use
audit should also be done in all the houses, residential and commercial buildings. The
Citizens of the UT may be encouraged to conserve water through rainwater harvesting,
recycling and reusing water and reducing water wastage. Pilot project for rain water

Poor Solid Waste Management system

Response of the Ministry
3.7.32 The Municipal Corporation, Chandigarh has already framed Chandigarh Municipal
Corporation (Sanitation and Public Health) Bye Laws, 1999. The Municipal Corporation Chandigarh

46
manages Solid Waste in 56 Sectors, 41 urban slums/colonies and 9 villages apart from erstwhile
N.A.C. Manimajra. Approximately 350 – 400 tonnes of Municipal Solid waste is generated per day

garbage and transfer it in the garbage bins. The Garbage is transported by deploying fast moving
dumper placers for 4.5 Cubic M Capacity containers. Tractor Trolleys, Refuse Collector
Compactors etc. are also pressed into service for transportation of garbage. To maintain the city
sanitation, 25 new Dumper placers and 200 new garbage bins have been procured in order to
provide aesthetic look of ‘City Beautiful’ and quick mobility of the Solid Waste from the city limits
for dumping. 200 Garbage bins have also been got repaired. The seasonal wastes i.e. dry leaves
etc. generated during the year are removed from the various Sectors/urban slums/colonies/villages
by deploying additional tractor trolleys with manpower so as to make the city free from the dry
leaves etc. The final disposal of the Municipal Solid Waste is done by processing the same through
Garbage Processing Plant which has been established on BOOT basis wherein the city garbage is
processed to form Refuse Derived Fuel (RDF). The Chandigarh Administration and the Municipal
Corporation took the initiative for commissioning of Garbage Processing Plant in the West of
Sector 25, Dadu Majra Chandigarh on BOOT (Built Own Operate and Transfer) basis to M/s Jai
Prakash Associates Ltd. wherein the plant management has set up the required machinery. All the
expenditure for setting up the Plant has been borne by the Project Developer. In view of the new
technology the same is being monitored for making the venture successful to produce Refuse
Derived Fuel to achieve the ultimate goal as to disposal and Processing of Municipal Solid Waste
as per the Municipal Solid Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2000. The Garbage Processing
Plant is processing approximately 250-300 MT Municipal Solid Waste everyday. The Management
of Garbage Processing Plant has also installed Hot Air Generator to process the wet garbage. The
monitoring of Garbage Processing Plant and Dumping Site is being looked after by the Engineering
Wing of Municipal Corporation, Chandigarh.
3.7.33 Reclamation of existing Dumping Site: The dumping site is spread in an area of 45 acres.
Out of this, 25 acres have been reclaimed scientifically as per the Municipal Solid Waste
(Management and handling) Rules, 2000. The landfill has been made in an approximate area of 8
acres and closing, covering and capping has been completed for approximately 17 acres with the
funds contributed by Central Pollution Control Board New Delhi, Chandigarh Administration and
Municipal Corporation, Chandigarh. The remaining 20 acres area is being used for dumping the
rejects/inerts from the Garbage Processing Plant and the waste coming from Sabzi Mandies,
ApniMandies, Big hotels, villages including villages under the Chandigarh Administration. The
dumped waste is leveled by using chain dozers. Effective Micro organism and micro nutrient
solution is sprayed three times a day over the waste to sanitize and make the garbage odourless.
A layer of malba/soil is spread over the waste using JCB, Tippers and chain dozers. The Dumping
Ground is properly fenced and buffer zone has been created around the Dumping Ground.
3.7.34 Installation of Bio Gas Plants: The Municipal Corporation (Engineering Wing) Chandigarh is
considering to install two Bio Gas Plants to Process the Hotel Waste, Vegetable Waste, mixed Waste
i.e. Horticulture and mixed garbage etc.
3.7.35 W ith the strenuous efforts made by the Municipal Corporation, Chandigarh to keep the City
Clean, Chandigarh has been adjudged as First by Ministry of Urban Development, on the basis of
National Rating Survey Data on City Sanitation in the recent past.
3.7.36 The Committee appreciates the solid waste management mechanism functional in
the UT. The Committee understands that solid waste management will be a key challenge
for any rapidly growing city. The Committee understands that for a viable solid waste
service delivery, the UT Administration should explore cost-effective environmental friendly

47
options to conserve natural resources and preserve landfill space, seek continuous

Drying up of Sukhnalake
3.7.51 There is likelihood of drying up of the Sukhnalake.

49
Response of the Ministry
3.7.52 Sukhna Lake is an artificial rain fed lake created in 1958. It has been observed that
whenever there is deficient rainfall in two successive years, the Sukhna Lake gets dried up for
about 1-2 months in the peak of summer months. This has happened 2-3 times in last 10 years.
However, the lake receives water as soon as monsoon arrives. There is no likelihood of Sukhna
Lake drying up permanently.
3.7.53 The Committee understands that Chandigarh is known for its famous Sukhna Lake
which is the most-visited tourist place in the area. With the lake not getting enough water
due to poor monsoon, it turns into a dried bed. As it is completely a rainfed lake
occasionally drying up due to periodic occurrence of deficit rainfall. The Committee
recommends that a think tank should be involved in this matter. Besides, There should be
a permanent body for its conservation and monitoring and its members should be drawn
from experts from the field of hydrology, soil, ecology, wildlife etc. A long term plan may

3.8 ISSUES CONCERNING ELECTRICITY DEPARTMENT
Privatization
3.8.1 It was demanded that the contemplated move to privatize/corporatize the Electricity
Department should be stopped as the move is against the interest of general public as well as
employees. Ever since the reorganization of the States and creation of Chandigarh in November,
1966, this Department has been functioning quite efficiently and is profit making, except last 2
years due to inefficiency of the controlling officers, even though the rates are less than that are
being charged in Punjab and Haryana. Electricity, being one of the most basic necessities for
growth of economy, had been kept in the hands of the government, either as a department or as
a state controlled public sector undertaking.
Response of the Ministry
3.8.2 Chandigarh Electricity Department (CED) is implementing the provisions of Electricity
Act, 2003 passed by the Parliament and the National Electricity Policy, 2005. In the Electricity
Act, 2003, reorganization of the board is provided under part-13 of the Act. Further, following
provisions have been provided under Para 5.4.3 of the Electricity Policy, 2005:
“5.4.3: For achieving efficiency gains proper restructuring of distribution utilities is
essential. Adequate transition financing support would also be necessary for these utilities.
Such support should be arranged linked to attainment of predetermined efficiency
improvements and reduction in cash losses and putting in place appropriate governance
structure for insulating the service providers from extraneous interference while at the same
time ensuring transparency and accountability. For ensuring financial viability and
sustainability, State Governments would need to restructure the liabilities of the State
Electricity Boards to ensure that the successor companies are not burdened with past
liabilities. The Central Government would also assist the States, which develop a clear road
map for turn around, in arranging transition financing from various sources which shall be
linked to predetermined improvements and efficiency gains aimed at attaining financial
viability and also putting in place appropriate governance structures.”
3.8.3 Therefore, Chandigarh Electricity Department is only implementing the provisions of the
Electricity Act, 2003/National Electricity Policy.

50
3.8.4 The Committee is of the view that while implementing the provisions of Electricity
Act, 2003 efforts should be made to protect the interests of the public and employees.
Inadequacy of Staff
3.8.5 The U.T. Powermen Union drew attention to the inadequacy of staff and equipments. The posts
that fell vacant have not been filled up and sanctioned posts to meet the increasing workload have
remained unfilled and even S.I.U. report has also not been implemented as the Central Government has
placed an embargo without any reasonable ‘justification’. These result in delay in extending services to
the public, giving rise to avoidable complaints. Administration was requested to consider these
shortcomings objectively to equip the Department to enable it to meet the demands of service of the
consumers as well as implementation of JERC decision i.e. standard of performance.
Response of the Ministry
3.8.6 The Electricity Department is regulated by the Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission.
Though CED requested to allow filling up of vacant posts but the JERC is not allowing filling up
of the vacant posts. Last year also, JERC has allowed filling up of 209  vacant posts for the
financial year 2012-13. A review petition was filed on this account which was also rejected by
the JERC. Again, the Department requested to allow to fill up 129 posts for the financial year
2013-14 but the JERC did not approve the same. Following orders have been passed in the tariff
order dated 15.04.2013 by the JERC for the financial year 2013-14 :
“---it is stated that considering an All India average number of employee per thousand
consumers is 0.405 ( i.e.  one employee per 2500 number of consumers). It can be
construed that the Electricity Department of Chandigarh is not understaffed. Hence, the
Commission does not consider and does not approve the manpower recruitment of nearly
129 employees for FY 2013-14. However, a few IT, Commercial and Accounts Officers
may be considered for recruitments in equal number as employees to fill the vacancies
created due to superannuation of employees and who will continue to provide the service
in line with the Standard of Performance of Distribution Code Regulations.”
3.8.7 The Committee desires that the issue of inadequacy of staff and equipments in the
Electricity Department may be resolved at the earliest.
3.9 ISSUES CONCERNING CHANDIGARH TRANSPORT UNDERTAKING
Vacant Posts
3.9.1 Posts of all the categories i.e. Drivers, Conductors, Workshops, Management Staff and
Class-IV staff are lying vacant in Chandigarh Transport Undertaking and no action towards the
requirement has been done so far.
Response of the Ministry
3.9.2 UT Administration has already conducted written test for the post of Drivers and declared
the result. However, the same has been challenged in the CAT in the Chandigarh. An advertisement
has been given for the recruitment of Conductors and the exam is likely to be held by the end
of October. As regards the recruitment of workshop staff, management staff, and Class-IV staff,
the cases are under active consideration of UT Administration.
3.9.3 The Committee recommends that UT Administration should conduct examination for
the recruitment of Conductors at the earliest. Besides, recruitment notification for vacant

51
posts of workshop staff, management staff, and Class-IV staff should also be advertised
soon and filled up at the earliest.
Purchase of new buses
3.9.4 The Management of the Chandigarh Transport Undertaking has not taken any initiative to
purchase new buses against the quota of replacement of buses despite the fact that the provision
of budget under the head of accounts has been granted.
Response of the Ministry
3.9.5 The matter regarding purchase of buses is under process by the UT Administration. The
tender has been floated.
3.9.6 The Committee is of the view that the UT Administration should complete the
process for procuring new buses without any procedural delay. The Committee believes that
non-availability of buses against sanctioned fleet will add woes to commuters.
Discrepancy in pay fixation
3.9.7 The workers have intimated that they have discrepancy in their pay fixation due to which
many junior staff in each cadre are getting higher pay as compared to their seniors.
Response of the Ministry
3.9.8 The pay fixation cases of the employees are being looked into by the UT Administration and
the anomalies are being removed as per rules.
3.9.9 The Committee recommends that the UT Administration should resolve the issue of
pay fixation of the employees as per rules at the earliest. The Committee would like to be
apprised of action taken in this regard.

recommends that the UT Administration should make all out efforts to project Daman
Ganga River Front as an important tourist destination and give due publicity to it so that
tourist flow to the UT could increase. (Para 1.3.5)

the issue of drinking water for the population as well as for industrial units. The

Vinoba Bhave Civil Hospital using new technologies. However, the Committee recommends
that the existing infrastructure in the said hospital should be upgraded for treatment of
chronic diseases. Sufficient fund may be provided for this purpose. The Committee

53
recommends that the administration should further improve health infrastructure in the
UT of Dadar and Nagar Haveli so that people residing in the UT could avail best health
facilities. (Para 1.3.12)
The Committee understands that Dairy Development is an important source to
enhance the level of income of small/marginal farmers and landless agricultural labourers
on a sustainable basis besides increasing milk supplies in the areas by increasing milk
production. The Committee recommends that Village Dairy Cooperatives should be opened
in every village of the UT which would help not only improve self sufficiency to the village
families but also enhance milk production and improve soil fertility and crop yields from
the manure obtained from animals. The Committee desires that more and more women
should be involved in the scheme as it would lead to their economic empowerment as well
as their participation in economic process. (Para 1.3.13)
The Committee notes the progress in the construction of 100 bedded Sub-District
Hospital to cater to the needs of people of Khanvel. The Committee desires that the
construction should be completed within stipulated time. (Para 1.3.17)
The Committee understands that Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) can play an
important role in the socio-economic development of rural people. The vast majority of our
country’s poorest people live in villages and these villages are in a state of neglect and
underdevelopment. The problems of hunger, ignorance, ill health, high mortality and
illiteracy are most acute in rural areas. In this context, the business houses can supplement
the efforts of Governments. (Para 1.3.21)

involving the industries through the Corporate Social Responsibility of adopting the
villages cautions that corporate should not be allowed to tamper with local culture, way
of life, etc. The Committee during the visit to the village noticed that most of the

is proposed to be changed. The UT Administration should remain vigilant to check if CSR
initiatives are according to local needs and sensitivity. The Corporate houses involved in
development should also respect local sensitivity in terms of their culture, way of life etc.
(Para 1.3.22)
The Committee takes note of the submission of the UT Administration that they
have requested the Ministry for further extension of tax benefits. The Committee
understands that due to the exemption of V AT, many big industries have set up plants in
this Union Territory leading to development in the Union Territory. The Committee
recommends that the proposal made by the UT Administration may be approved so that
industrial development may continue to grow in the UT. (Para 1.4.7)
The Committee is aware of the fact that despite India being an attractive investment
destination, entire exercise of the procedure and legal formalities make it tedious and
confusing. The Committee is of the view that long legal formalities and procedural delays
make frustrating impact on the investors. The Committee recommends that UT
administration should introduce single window composite application form for all the
procedural clearances such as acquiring land, granting of construction permission, pollution
control procedures, issuing occupancy certificates, power allocation, environment and forest
clearances and other licences/registrations which would make this region investment
friendly and boost industrial growth in the UT. The Committee also recommends that
suggestions/views of representatives of industry and trade associations should also be taken
into account while framing policies and laws pertaining to industries as they are the people

who know what are the bottlenecks coming in their way. The Committee also recommends
that the Ministry of Home Affairs should positively consider the demands of representatives
of trade and industry as subsidies given would provide stimuli for further industrialization.

restored. The Committee also recommends that the 25 MW with drawn may also be
restored. (Para 1.4.10)

Environment and Forest for sparing 100 mtrs. as a sensitive zone. The Committee is of the
opinion that this territory is very small and for the development of this territory it will be
virtually impossible to have industries or any other development activities in view of having
eco-sensitive zones of 10 kms around. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry
of Home Affairs should remind the Ministry of Environment and Forest for early clearance
of the issue. Otherwise this policy will lead to driving out the industries and developmental
works of the UT will come to a stall. (Para 1.4.14)
The Committee recommends that the UT Administration should grant Licences as per
Rules and Regulations and there should not be any discrimination in the process. An early
decision may be taken in the matter. (Para 1.4.17)
The Committee takes note of the concerns of the villagers of Naroli village and

look into the matter. The Authorities involved should adopt a balancing approach and try
their best to minimize negative impart. The issues relating to displacement and
compensation may be looked into. (Para 1.5.3)
The Committee takes note of the reply and recommends that The UT Administration
while sanctioning posts, the interests of the Daman & Diu and Dadra & Nagar Haveli
Administration Services should be kept in view. (Para 1.5.6)
The Committee takes note of the submission made by the UT Administration. The
Committee notes that for the last five years the allocation to the district panchayat of UT
of Dadra and Nagar Haveli is on the increase and hopes that this trend will continue in
future. The Committee hopes that increase will help financing of the important projects of
district panchayat. (Para 1.5.9)

filing up of vacancies is also simultaneously under examination. The Committee
recommends that the matter of filling up of vacant post should be decided on priority and
filled up at the earliest. The matter of creation of posts also needs to be expedited. An early
decision may be taken in the matter. (Para 1.5.12)

for expediting of opening medical College in Silvassa. The Committee desires that the
medical college should start working from the next academic session. (Para 1.5.14)

the same way the Administrator is also the Head of a UT. The Committee recommends that
the financial powers of the Administrator should be enhanced appropriately so that various
important decisions could be taken at the Administrator level. In view of the Committee
this will result in fast approval and implementation of all major projects for the UTs and
avoid cost escalation due to time overruns. (Para 1.5.16)

55
The Committee notes with appreciation that T&D power loss in Daman and Diu UT
is among the lowest in the country and tariffs are among the lowest in the western region
with all villages electrified. The Committee also notes that 93% electricity consumption is
in industry sector. The Committee was also given to understand that 37 km. underground
cabling has been completed. Besides, setting up of different electricity sub stations, 4 MW
solar plants (3MW in Diu and 1 MW in Daman) are proposed to be set up. The Committee
recommends that need of the industries for power should be met so as to maintain the
tempo of economic development. Project of clean energy in the field of solar  energy should
be completed without time and cost overruns. Other sources of clean energy like wind
energy should also be explored. (Para 2.3.5)

of electricity charges should be decided in a very balanced manner so that while on one
hand it should not cause disincentive for industries in view of the special position of the
UT where various measures such as tax benefits, etc. are given to industries for setting up
their units in the UT, on the other hand, it should not make the power supplying entity a
loss making one. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should
look into the matter very cautiously. (Para 2.3.8)

connectivity of various parts/areas of Daman and its adjoining areas by constructing new

strengthen coastal policing in the UT. After the Mumbai terror attack, coastal security has

demand for a national stadium in the UT. (Para 2.4.10)
